utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning. It's Joanna Korner, Alex Demirdjian and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. The co-Defence counsel and the Defence team of Mico Stanisic, Slobodan Cvijetic and Eugene O'Sullivan, legal advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence this morning, Igor Pantelic, Dragan Krgovic, and I have special honour to announce Ms. Michelle Butler, our legal consultant, and just for the record, special legal weapon for Defence against the Prosecution. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we revert this morning, before Mr. Gasi comes back, to Your Honours' ruling yesterday, and we are seeking clarification. We did ask for a written decision, and I believe Mr. O'Sullivan wants to address Your Honours on the matter, but from our point of view, what Judge Harhoff said yesterday was this: "The Chamber may decide whether she is an expert or not. On this question, the Chamber has deliberated and ruled. She is qualified as an expert. The next question is what to do then with her report. You will bring it under Rule 94 bis as an expert report, and it is for the Defence to challenge. If at the end of the challenge raised by the Defence, the Chamber finds that there is really nothing of substantive value in this report, just as an example, then of course the Chamber has to be free to say we will not admit the report or at least not all of it." Your Honours, what is still, I am afraid, unclear to us, is whether Your Honours are admitting the report under Rule 94 so that it can go in as an exhibit, and then deciding, having heard the evidence, what weight to attach to which parts of the report. Because, Your Honour Judge Harhoff, used the word "will decide" whether to admit and that's what we are just querying. In other words, when Ms. Hanson is called, as with other experts, does her report as she is called go in as an exhibit and then we deal with such parts of it as we think relevant and the Defence deal with other parts. So that you then decide what weight, if any, you attach to such parts of the report. That's our query this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The practical way of viewing our ruling yesterday is that the -- having deemed her as an expert, by virtue of that fact, her report becomes admissible. Everything after that is a question of weight. So we would -- as the Chamber, we would have to see what is -- what to make of that report after especially cross-examination. So her report is in but everything thereafter is a question of weight.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honours, that's helpful. Before I deal with the practical consequences of this, I think Mr. O'Sullivan has something to say on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. The -- for the record, yesterday at the conclusion of the discussion on this, Judge Harhoff said that if the parties requested it there would be a written ruling, and yesterday the parties did informally contact the Chamber by e-mail requesting a written ruling and I wish just to place that request on the record. It came both from the Prosecution and the Defence for a written ruling. Our intention is to seek certification of your decision and under Rule 73(C), our certification must be filed with you within seven days of your written ruling. That being the case, we would wish to request a stay of the testimony of this witness until there has been a ruling on our request for certification. This witness should not be heard because we, with all due respect, wish to challenge your ruling on appeal and we were seeking your leave for certification to bring this before the Appeals Chamber. So we say that the witness shall not be heard pending the ruling on your behalf on our request for certification which will follow your written ruling.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I assist on the timing?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I was going to say was, in any event, we foresee enormous difficulties in calling Ms. Hanson this week now. We've still got this witness, who is still in chief, another witness to follow and I think the estimate of cross-examination was not less than a couple of hours and he is a couple of hours in chief. We are not sitting beyond, as I understand it, Thursday lunch time, tomorrow lunch time. We have an unmovable witness on Monday, followed by two further unmovable witnesses, and big witnesses, who are answering summonses on Tuesday and Thursday of next week. So the reality is, we wouldn't, in any event, be able to put Ms. Hanson in. So that's why I thought I'd better tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So in essence, you would agree to the proposal made by the Defence that they be given their full seven days to respond in good order to the written ruling that we are going to hand down very shortly?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, as a matter of -- that's what I was going to say, as a matter of practical reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you also request then two weeks in addition to respond to the motion made by the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, we'll respond very quickly to that, Your Honour. We only requested that the proper time for the intercept motion, but if an appeal -- if an application for leave to appeal is filed, we will respond very quickly. I think the actual consequences of all of this is, at Your Honours' urging, we've literally stacked -- as we've discovered when Judge Delvoie worked out the timings on our witness, we have witnesses stacked between now and Christmas, subject to all the usual things going wrong. So it's unlikely, I anticipate, that you will be hearing from Ms. Hanson before the Christmas break, unless something goes very wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please have the witness return to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gasi. I will remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Morning, Mr. Gasi.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to start off by showing you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May the witness be shown 65 ter 320, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, this is a document that was shown to you, I believe in the Krajisnik case. It is a summary by the War Presidency of the municipality of Brcko. It deals with the background of the conflict, the Assembly session we talked about yesterday, the blowing of the bridge, et cetera. Now, you hadn't seen this document at the time; is that correct? When I say "at the time" I mean in 1992.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to go to the last numbered page and show the witness the signature block on this document. The page previous to that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's the signature of Djordje Ristanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you remind the Trial Chamber who Djordje Ristanic was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the War Presidency of the municipality of Brcko, and I know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us whether the signature is in Cyrillic or in Latin letters?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Cyrillic letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how do you know Mr. Ristanic?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to primary school together at Brcko from the 1st to the 8th form. And when I went to the secondary electrician school, he went to another vocational school. So I know him well and we grew up together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to page 3 in the B/C/S, and in English it is page 2, middle of the page. Now, on this page, Witness, there's a reference to members of the "Zelene Beretke," the Green Berets. Are you able to locate that on that page? Page 3, I believe it's the third paragraph in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we can scroll up just a little bit. I apologise, can we scroll up a little bit more? Scroll up. This is page 2. Page 3, please, on the document. I apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see the third paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This paragraph starts with: "Members of the Green Berets placing barricades in areas bordering Serbian parts of the city, cutting the main roads towards Loncari, Bosanski Samac and Modrica." Now in 1992 did you have a chance to drive around the town of Brcko during the months of April and May?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was -- I had a chance to move about almost in the entire territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what can you tell us about this paragraph talking about barricades by the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't see barricades put up by the Green Berets at that time at Brcko. That goes for all of April and the part of May when I was in -- either in my apartment or later at the Elektrodistribucija centre at Brcko, I never saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just so the Trial Chamber understands, when you were working for Elektro Brcko in the month of May, can you explain your travels during that month?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, the furthest I went was to the vicinity of the place mentioned here in this report, it's on the main road from the Brcko hospital toward Mujkici and Gluhakovac. These are the local communities. They aren't mentioned here. But it's the road that goes in that direction. It was on the 11th or the 12th of May, possibly the 13th of May. But I didn't see any barricades. There were damaged houses in that part of town and broken glass and damaged vehicles along that main road, but barricades, no, I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we move to -- in the B/C/S page number 4. And it's 4 on the top of the page. And in English page 3, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, while we wait for this to come up, could we just ascertain from the witness whether he saw -- whether his testimony is that he didn't see any barricades at all, because I think your question was whether he saw any barricades set up by the Green Berets. The question could be, well, did he see other barricades such as ones set up by the Crisis Staff of the Serbs, or any other barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Witness, you heard the question by Judge Harhoff. Do you remember seeing any other barricades in and around the town of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war started in Brcko, throughout the month of April, they put up the so-called check-points, security points manned by the civilian police and the military police from the Brcko garrison. That was before the war, throughout the month of April almost. And during the war - when I say "war," I mean from the 1st of May up to the 13th of May - as I was moving through town, there were still check-points but the composition of people at those check-points was not mixed. There were people in camouflage uniforms from the Brcko garrison and members of the Territorial Defence, I suppose they were Serbs. And there were some other men from the police station in Brcko. They were present all over the town. Wherever you moved about there were three or four or five people on every road who stopped you, asked you for your ID, asked you where you were headed, who had approved your movement, what was your reason for going to that particular part of town and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: At page 8, line 8, I believe it reads that those check-points were not mixed. Witness, can you clarify, you just told us that you saw camouflage uniforms, TO members, police members. Did you mean to say that the check-points were mixed or were not mixed? Perhaps it's a lost-in-translation issue.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, in the month of April 1992, they were mixed with the members of the civilian police, and when I say "mixed," I mean national composition. If there were members from the Brcko SUP, then that means that there were Croats, Serbs and Muslims, and they were combined with the members of the military police from the garrison. In the month of May, I did not see that kind of check-points in Brcko. They were all members of one ethnic group and that's what I meant when I said that they were no longer mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, can I take you now at page 4, the second paragraph from the bottom, and in English it's page 3, the third paragraph. Do you see discussions about: "When the war begun and the public security station was taken over, the same day the War Presidency appointed Dragan Veselic, chief of the public security station ..." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you know Dragan Veselic?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Since when do you know him?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've known him since before the war in Brcko, a couple of years before the war. I believe that we were engaged in some conversations with other people who know him. I believe that we even had a cup of coffee or two together in one of the cafe bars in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What was his occupation prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was mathematics and physics teacher at the Brcko grammar school known as the Vaso Pelagic school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if he had any training, any police training prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think so. I would be surprised to know that Veselic had any police training.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you know whether around the elections in 1990 or after the elections if he belonged to any of the political parties?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. I believe that he was an SDS member, the Serbian Democratic Party in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If you look at that paragraph, it carries on and says that after the appointment of Dragan Veselic: "... began the staffing of the station with new people, including Serbs who had been employed there before." And it continues by: "The problem was the same as the army. Most of them were not trained to work as policemen, but there was no option." Can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the reason was to replenish the police station in Brcko. Already at that time the same men who had worked there before the war, and I'm referring to the ethnic composition, they were again brought back to continue working. Whether they stopped working before the war or not, I don't know. I don't think that anything ever changed, either before he was appointed the chief of the SUP or thereafter. As far as I can remember and as far as I could observe around the town, I don't know if anything was changed either before or in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I take you at the top of page number 5 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, can the top of page 5 be displayed to the witness, please. And in English that's still page 3, second and third paragraph from the bottom. The page has a 5 on the top of the page. Next one in B/C/S. Next one. Does it show page number 5 at the top of the page. Can we scroll up? Okay, if we can scroll up to the top of the page. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, do you see a section there that deals with the largest part of the Serbian forces came from Semberija, Bijeljina, Ugljevik?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And for the English, if we can just scroll down a little bit, please, for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The paragraph continues and says that: "They were mainly organised in two formations, the Serbian guard under the command of Ljubisa Savic, aka Mauzer, and the radicals under the command of Mirko Blagojevic." Did you have a chance to meet Mr. Savic, aka Mauzer, in 1992 in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have an occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Trial Chamber the occasion on which you met Mr. Mauzer?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One day in the month of May while I was still working at Elektrodistibucija, that gentleman came. In the company of two other members of his unit, he came to the Elektrodistribucija. He had a chat with our director. And he then he called all the staff who were at the Elektrodistribucija at the time, and they lined up in files -- they lined us up in files of two and then we heard a political speech delivered by Mr. Mauzer. And that was my meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did he address you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went from one man to the next as we were lined up as if we were in the army. He asked everybody what our names were. Most of us, maybe six or seven -- or rather, most of us were Muslims, six or seven were Serbs, and there were two Croats. And as I said, he went from one man to the next. He asked our names. He came up to me, asked me what my name was. I said Isak and then he moved on. He did not ill treat me either verbally or physically at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did he say anything to your group? You've explained to us that he had the Croats and the Muslims on one side?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on when he was done doing that, there was a colleague of ours who was Serb and he was with us and he said we should be separated. The Serbians to one side and the Muslims to the other side. The Serb colleague stayed with us. He came up to that Serb colleague, asked him what his name was. The colleague answered. And then he said, What are you doing with the balijas here? And he answered, Well, they are my colleagues, my work colleagues. Then he asked again, What was your name again, to which he answered. And then he said, Well, your brother got killed and the likes of those in Elektrodistribucija killed him. And the guy said, No, they didn't, I'm staying with them. And that was the discussion which resulted in the ill treatment of us non-Serbs. And then, after that, he changed his discourse because he remembered who the brother of that electrician was and then he came up to the director and members of the Serb people and started talking to them, we couldn't hear that conversation and he told the rest of us that we could go, that we were no longer needed. And that's how the whole event ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, my learned friend. It's page 12, line 18, the sentence is starting: "And that was the discussion which resulted in the ill treatment of us non-Serbs." I think we heard something else. Could you clarify that with the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Line 13, isn't it, the discussion with the ill treatment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Witness, I don't know if you see it on the screen, it says: "... discussion which resulted in the ill treatment of us non-Serbs." Can you clarify that for us? Counsel seems to think something else was said. Or is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Verbal ill treatment, Mr. Pantelic, consisted in somebody walking behind your back with a Scorpion gun and then shouts at you in loud voice, What is your name? And then you say Ibro, Sulja or Husa. Now whether you would call that verbal ill treatment or physical ill treatment, I don't know. In any case, that's how things transpired. Dusko Tuzlancic, who followed him at the time, had a shot-gun and he turned the barrel towards the group where I was standing and he started playing with the bullet. He -- that was the kind of ill treatment we suffered. But I never said that anybody was hit with a rifle-butt, a Mauzer rifle-butt, or that Dusko Tuzlancic did that. No, they didn't. But it was not a pleasant thing to hear somebody say to you "balija" or things like that. And the ill treatment that I mentioned was that sense. I really did not feel comfortable, I must say, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, can you look at the next paragraph which starts with: "The first to arrive in Brcko was the group of instructors of Captain Dragan." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In the middle of the paragraph there's a sentence that reads: "When the war started and during the combat activities, a number of members of this unit joined the police intervention platoon, but the special unit grew to about 70 people." What do you know about the police intervention platoon?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a neighbour of mine, in the month of April, was a member of that Special Police. His name was Ranko Cesic and he lived in the same building as I did. Miso Cajevic was also a member of that unit. I know that two brothers from the same building where I lived also belonged to the same unit. One of the brothers, a neighbour of mine, his name is Predrag, I believe, personally told me that he had participated in the liberation of Bosanski Samac. Ranko Cesic and Miso Cajevic, whom I both saw in Luka wearing police uniforms, light blue uniforms, they were later on transferred from that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, this paragraph says that a number of members of these paramilitary units joined the intervention -- the police intervention platoon. What can you say to us about the relationship between the police and these paramilitary groups in Brcko in the month of April and May 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the town itself, in the course of the month of April, before the bridge on the Sava was blown up, if you were moving anywhere near the town centre, a lot of people did walk around during the month of April. You could see members of those units. They often came to the Brcko SUP. They parked their vehicles in front of the Brcko police station. And the purpose of all that was the establishment of joint patrols and joint mixed check-points at the exits from the town of Brcko in both directions. This is what I saw and noticed in Brcko at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to show you one last extract from this document at page 8 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The top paragraph. When I say page 8, it's again the page number 8 on the document. And in English it's page 5, the fourth, fifth, and sixth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Are you able to see the document, Mr. Gasi?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you see it starting with: "The result of looting is that Brcko is now a devastated town." Is that the first sentence you see on that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, the paragraph deals with stealing and seizing cars, looting by various units, and the last sentence of that paragraph says: "Locals joined those teams and the police were unable to prevents this, and some of them probably joined in." Can you tell us anything about the looting in the town of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion between the 1st of May and the 10th of May, while I was in my apartment, the street where I lived was next to the garrison. A vehicle came by with loud-speakers inviting people who felt threatened by combat activities to come out of their apartments because they would be transported to the garrison of the JNA in Brcko. And people did come out, and I was observing that from the window of my apartment. And my -- a neighbour of mine told me, Don't move anywhere from your apartment. Then military truck came, they picked up all the people from private houses and they took them away. I suppose they took them to the garrison. An hour later, a few more trucks came and started taking things from those houses. A few days later, those people who had been taken to the garrison came back. They were returned to their homes. This is what I could observe at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The people that were taken out, can you tell us, if you know, what was their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people residing in residential houses across the road from my building were Muslims. The name of that street was Blagoje Simikic Street before the war. I don't know what it's called now. The names change all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask for that document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness did not recognise the document. He is not the author of the document. He doesn't know anything about the document. He never saw it. The only thing that he recognised on the document is the signature of the document's author, and that's all. The Prosecutor used the opportunity to talk to him about the events, but we don't think that this document can be admitted through the witness. There were -- there will be other people from the police, from the War Presidency, who will be more competent and better suited to talk about that document. We will perhaps even have the author of the document himself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I just add something. We don't know at this stage if the author will be called. We are not calling him. May I just point out to the Judges that this document in terms of relevance, I think the witness has covered the relevance. In terms of reliability, he has authenticated the signature of the author. Although he hasn't seen the document at that time, he is familiar with the underlying facts. At this stage I would say it's a matter for the Judges discretion under Rule 89(C) which he covered extensively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic's objection is noted, but in the Chamber's view, the document is admissible and it may be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P129, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, you mentioned in your testimony in the Krajisnik case, and this is at page 422 of the Krajisnik transcript, that you witnessed killings on the 6th or the 7th of May at the marketplace. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do indeed. It was not at the marketplace itself. It was on one of the streets leading to the marketplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you mentioned, at page 424 of the Krajisnik transcript, seeing a policeman wearing a blue uniform shooting at three civilians in their heads. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May the witness be shown 65 ter 2163. And may I just note for Your Honours that this is one of the three documents that were in the 92 ter package for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see the image on your screen, Mr. Gasi?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise the area?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what -- which part of town is this?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the very centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Is this where you were on the 6th or 7th of May when you witnessed the shootings?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May we have the assistance of the usher so that the witness can mark this image.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, can you indicate to the Court with the pen in which building you were when you witnessed the shootings? Can you mark that with a 1?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I know it's not very easy to draw on that board. Yes. And can you indicate to us where you saw the policeman shooting at the three civilians?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you mark that with a 2.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately what is the distance between the building and the area where you saw the shootings?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe 30 to 40 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: From that distance, were you capable of identifying the policeman?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He had his back turned to me, and later on they moved to a different street around the corner and I could no longer see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May this photo be seized and admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P130, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And may the witness be shown the next photograph, 65 ter 2167.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see the photo, Mr. Gasi?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is this image?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now we can see the street where the building is on the left-hand side with the damaged facade. That's where all that happened. Here, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If you could mark the area where you saw the three civilians killed.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you just mark that with a 1.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And may that be captured and admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P131, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May the witness be shown the next photograph, which is 65 ter 2164.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see the photo, Mr. Gasi?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Is this the same street that we just saw earlier?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The policeman you saw on that day, was he wearing a similar uniform as the man we see on the right with the blue shirt?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same a uniform. The same kind of uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This was not the man that you saw, however, just to be clear?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that's the very man, but I do remember that he had a bandaged arm -- or rather, I would have remembered if he had a bandaged arm such as this one in the picture has.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May the witness be shown the next photograph -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. As Exhibit P132, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May the witness be shown 65 ter 2165.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Witness, is this the same street that we were discussing?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And again, this is the same uniform that the policeman you saw was wearing on the 7th of May?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: There's actually a third photograph in this series, perhaps we can put them in one bundle, put tab 1, tab 2, tab 3. If we can show the next photograph which is 65 ter 2166.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Once again, this is the same street, Mr. Gasi?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, while you were in Brcko during the month of May, this uniform, was it a uniform you regularly saw?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a pre-war police uniform like those --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The police wore such uniforms before the war and I believe during the war too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And these three photos that we just showed you, would you happen to know who took those photographs?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us who that person was?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Bojan Stojanovic, a reporter, photo reporter from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how do you know that he took those very photographs?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July 1992, when I was in Belgrade, Rade Bosic brought him to that friend of mine and he came with a folder full of photographs that he had taken during the war at Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And he showed you those photos?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. And others too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May that last photograph be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. These photographs will be admitted and marked sequentially, not as a package, for certain administrative reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's perfectly fine.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P133 and Exhibit P134, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, you told the Court in the Krajisnik case that during the month of May you were asked to work for Elektro Brcko; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And that you had to stay at the Elektro Brcko building, eat and sleep there, 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: On one occasion you told the Court, and this was at page 435 and 436 of the Krajisnik transcript, that you had to work on a transformer pole?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be precise, we are speaking about high-voltage electricity poles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And is it correct that you had to climb up this pole?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We did climb up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Approximately how high was this pole?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I ask the Court Officer to display on the screen 65 ter 2170.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, do you recognise this photo?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you tell us what this photo is?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know exactly where this place is. Very close to this spot we worked on those high-voltage poles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And from the high-voltage pole you had climbed, were you able to see this grave?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not this one. I saw another.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this grave itself, where was it in relation to the pole that you had to climb up?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, it was 150 to 200 metres away from the pole where I was. I mean, this very grave we are looking at now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the grave that you were able to see from the pole, how does it compare to this image?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one would be behind my back if I were on the pole now. And the other I mentioned would be in front of me. So I would be facing the other and this one would be behind my back. Unless I lost my sense of orientation due to the lapse of time. Yes, I do think that this one would be behind my back and the -- I would be facing the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: On the top right-hand corner of the photo, there is part of a truck. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you recognise this truck?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can recognise it. It used to drive down the main road that passed by the Elektrodistribucija where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It is correct in the Krajisnik case that you stated that you had seen this truck go back and forth while you were working at Elektro Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It would probably pass in one direction in the morning and go back later, but there were days when it passed to and fro twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And on some occasions, did you recognise the driver?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. I think that I saw a man whom I knew before the war twice. He worked at the police station at Brcko before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you indicate to the Court what his name is?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mika Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could this photo be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P135, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, you mentioned to us, in the Krajisnik case again at page 440, that you worked at Elektro Brcko between the 10th and the 27th of May, 1992, and you also stated that you were arrested on the 27th of May at your place of work. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court who arrested you on that day?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two police officers. One was a professional police officer. He had been with the police before the war at Brcko. And the other was a reserve officer before the war, probably during the war became an active serviceman with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what were their names?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The professional was Dragan Pantelic, and the other was Stevo Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When you were arrested, were you given any reasons for your arrest?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they stated no reasons to me, and when they arrived at the entrance gate, where an office is, where the electrician on duty was, and the director of the company, Miodrag Ristic, was there too. They approached them first and asked if I was here, and they confirmed. And I was in the warehouse some maybe 20 metres away from that office, and I went there, and the director said to me, Well, the police is here, they have come for you. And before they put me in that vehicle, he asked -- the director asked them, where are you taking him and why? And I think it was Stevo, and possibly Dragan, who said if someone comes asking for them -- for him, just tell them that the Serbian police has taken him away. And that was all. They put me in the vehicle and took me to the police station at Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May the witness be shown 65 ter 2161.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, do you see the photo on your screen?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this building and can you tell us what is this building?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the Brcko police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this is where Mr. Pantelic and Mr. Knezevic took you on the 27th of May?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were you brought inside the police station?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As you see, this is the main entrance, and we entered there, and to the right, there is a reception desk. They took me into a room. They called it Room 13. Actually, they bounced me into it, pushed me into it. It's on the right-hand side viewed from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you entered the police station and you saw the reception area, did you see any policemen?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There may have been six or seven police officers in regular police uniforms in that reception office, and in that wider part of the entrance I saw also some people in civilian clothes and members of the regular police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I offer this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P136, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if the witness can be shown the next document, 65 ter 2162.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see the image on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What can we see on this image?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a photograph of that room, number 13 they called it, where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And is this how it looked in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I offer this image, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P137, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: How long were you held in this room, Mr. Gasi?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not longer than -- or actually less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that after an hour, you were taken to another detention centre?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that this was the Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In the Krajisnik case you deal with your detention at the Luka camp as of page 443.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if we may show the witness the next photograph, which is 2156. 65 ter 2156.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this image?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Before I get into the Luka camp, can you quickly tell us, if you know, what is the distance between the police station and the Luka camp, approximately, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: 300 to 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Luka camp, you told us in the Krajisnik case, and that's at page 445, that a man named Pudic hit you. Can you describe this event, this incident?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was waiting for me in front of the first office, here where the hangars begin. He was there already and when I got out of the vehicle, he immediately started shouting and asking about Muslim barricades. He mentioned some family names such as Islamovic and Jasikovic and I had never heard of these people before and I replied, What you are you talking about, man? And then he took his pistol and started pushing me and hit me behind the neck and pushed me into a hallway where that office was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, if it's possible to mark this image, if you can show us where Mr. Pudic was when you entered Luka camp.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If you can mark that with a number 1.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And secondly, if you can indicate to us which office he pushed you in?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was right here at the same spot, in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the first name of Mr. Pudic?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Branko.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Pudic before the war?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him personally. I only knew him by sight, and I know he was a police officer at Brcko. He also lived in the same part of town as my parents-in-law, and he used to -- and I used to see him around. I know that he was a police officer, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall what he was wearing on that day?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A regular police uniform, as any normal or regular police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: How long were you in that office with Mr. Pudic?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment I entered, the entire conversation lasted about 30 or 40 minutes, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what happened after these 30 or 40 minutes?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I entered the office, there were another four men. On the right there was one with a large beard. He was wearing a cockade, and one was wearing a JNA uniform, and one was wearing a fire -- or carrying a fire hose. One of them was wearing a camouflage uniform, and in the centre of that office there was a table at which two people were sitting facing each other. I knew one of them. And the other I had never seen. The one to the right of that table was wearing an old reserve uniform of the JNA with the rank of a 2nd lieutenant. And when they pushed me inside, I said good afternoon. And the bearded guy jumped up and said, What is this, good afternoon? Don't you know how the Serbian brethren greet each other? And I said [B/C/S spoken] and he replied, You see, he knows. And they were saying, Where was this one on Kosovo engaged in counter-revolution. And in that office there was another friend of mine, a Serb from Brcko who was an active captain at the JNA who said, Come off it, stop it already. I know the man. He is an active sportsman, and started speaking about my sporting achievements. And then the situation changed somewhat, and the one -- the 2nd lieutenant who was sitting said to Pudic, Pudic, take him away to the hanger and then we'll see what we do with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Where were you taken next, were you taken to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you mark on this image where this was?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And mark that with a number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this is where you were detained on that day?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pudic took me in and on the right from the place where we entered the hangar, there was a chair. The entire hangar was empty. He said, You see that chair, sit on it and don't budge, and don't look around either, and I'll be back and then we'll see what will happen. And then after some 20 minutes, Pudic came back and he said to me, Now go to the other part of the hangar which is separated from this number 2, or rather, connected with a large gate. And I was looking to the left and to the right. There were people lying there on the concrete floor. And he said to me, Find yourself a place. And that's how I entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us in the Krajisnik case at page 460 that that day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Counsel, at what point would it be convenient to break.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: At what point would it be --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Are you -- I thought you were finished with this photograph and I was going to invite you to take the break at that point, but you seem to be going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I agree. We could actually tender this photograph and I can continue after the break with the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P138, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is coming in, there's just one small procedural matter. We have been alerted that the record is somewhat unclear as to where we stand in terms of what the Chamber has decided with respect to the witness Hanson. As we would have indicated, the written decision will be, we trust, available tomorrow. And then things will follow in their ordinary sequence. So whereas it appears that implicitly we have acceded to the application by the Defence for a stay of her testifying, as I said, after tomorrow's ruling, then we would hear from the parties and things would follow their natural course. But it is obvious from what will have passed before that she is not coming this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, before the break we were talking about the time when you were brought to the Luka camp and you indicated to us that you were hit by Mr. Branko Pudic. Did there come a time later on in that day where you were dealing a man named Ivan?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And at page 468 in the Krajisnik case, you indicated to us that he was wearing the insignia of Arkan's men?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe that incident for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivan came to the hangar accompanied by two other men and then he stood in front of them in the middle of the hangar. And he asked aloud, Where is that Siptar that came today? I didn't respond immediately. Across the hangar from me there were two men of Albanian origin, just like me. Their parents hailed from Kosova, just like mine. That's why I didn't respond immediately. Let me -- and then he says, Let me repeat, where is that Siptar, the athlete that came today? And then I stood up, and then he says, Come closer to me. And I came closer, maybe 2 or 3 metres away from me. And he then he said even closer. And then he asked me, What is your nationality? And I answered I'm a Yugoslav. And then at that moment he came up to me, he was holding his right arm behind his back, and then he said, Where is that Yugoslavia of yours now? And then he hit him [as interpreted], he was aiming at my head but he missed and he hit me here and then he hit me in the shoulder. I fell on the ground and then he started kicking me. One of the men who were with him grabbed me by the jumper and lifted me. One of them took the pistol out of the bolster, put it in my mouth, he wanted to fire a bullet but there was no bullet in the pistol. And then he said, This time you are lucky, but the next time I'm going to have a bullet for you. The man who was holding me let me go. I fell down on the ground and I remained lying there for awhile. That was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What was the instrument that he used to hit you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he hit me with a metal implement for screwing and unscrewing firemen's hoses. When there is a fire, that's what the firemen will use to secure the hoses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And after this incident, Mr. Gasi, were you beaten again during your time at the Luka camp, and you told us you were there between the 27th of May and the 7th of June, so during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't beat me but Goran once took me out -- actually, it was Kosta who wanted to see me in his office. Then they tied me to a chair and Goran started showing off with his knife, which he threw at me, and he threw the knife next to me. And he said, I'm not going to use the pistol, I'm going to use the knife. I'm going to cut off your hands and feet first. Then Goran said, We are not going to do anything to him tonight. Then they took me out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned two names, you mentioned Kosta first of all. Can you tell the Court who is Kosta, and what is his full name, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a local Serb from Brcko. Before the war, I believe he was a decorator. And during the war he wore a police uniform. And when I was taken to Luka, I saw him on the following day, immediately the day after. He introduced himself as somebody who was the deputy commander of the Luka camp, or the investigating prison as he called him. He was wearing a police uniform all the time. His name is Konstantin Simeunovic and in Brcko we refer to him as Kole, that was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the other person you mentioned was Goran. Can you tell us who Goran is and his full name, please?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Jelisic. He also had a nickname. Adolf, that's what he used to call himself when he came to the hangar. He came twice before the incident involving me, and every time he wore a camouflage uniform. And on that a particular evening, I believe that he was wearing a blue shirt. I don't know whether it was a short-sleeved or a long-sleeved police uniform, and I saw that he had one star as -- of the kind that the police inspector would have. That's all I can remember at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, you told us by Goran Jelisic --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just for Your Honours' information, Goran Jelisic was accused and sentenced by this Tribunal several years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What did Jelisic do exactly with the knife? If you could just clarify that area.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nothing. But Kosta brought me in. He asked him, Is that the guy who is playing smart, because Kosta asked me about the names of some Muslim extremists. Before that I had a stomach-ache and I had diarrhoea at the time, he said, Isak, I'm going to give you a lot of tablets but if you give me a lot of names of Muslim extremists. And then I said, I'm going to give you ten names. And he says, how come? And then I said, Just bring me a piece of paper and I will give you the names. And then I gave him the names of all the members of the SDA board in Brcko, but all those people had fled Brcko before the war. And then he gave me the tablets. A couple of days after that he came at dusk and he says, Okay, come with me, Isak. And then Goran says, Is that the guy who is playing smart? And he says yes. And then he says, Okay, tie him to the chair. Kosta then handcuffed me and tied me to the chair. And then he said, I'm not going to use the gun, I'm going to use the knife. I'm going to cut off your -- both hands and feet. I will leave you like that and then I'll slaughter you. And then when Kosta tied me on the chair, then he approached me from the left side and knifed me lightly on the left-hand side two or three times. And after that he says, Okay, you can take him out now, we'll finish him off later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When Kosta asked you for those names, was he alone or was there other people during this exchange when he promised he would give you tablets?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another man. That happened once when they allowed me to go out. Sometimes they would allow you to go out and go to the toilet, and there was a bathroom in a different part of the building where their offices were. Kosta encountered me there and he realised even a few days before that I had problems with my stomach and that's how the dialogue started. I suppose that there were other people in the offices listening in. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, we need you to slow down a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: For the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, did there come a time where you were interrogated at the Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the following day, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petar Kaurinovic put questions to me in the presence of Zoran Kontic and Pero Zaric. I know the three of them. Petar Kaurinovic used to work in the Brcko police before the war. He was a crime inspector. Zoran Kontic was a forensic technician who used to take photos of incidents and traffic accidents. And Pero Zaric was an athlete whom I had known before the war in Brcko, but he was not a policeman there in Brcko at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what was Petar Kaurinovic wearing on that day when he interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian clothes. Pero Zaric and Zoran Kontic wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May we display on the screen 65 ter 2138, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gasi, I'm going to show you a list of names, and this is a list of employees of the Brcko police station. It is dated the month of September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is the only SJB Brcko document we actually have, the only list we do have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You can see on the first page that this document is dated the 7th of October, 1992. And is it -- it is correct to say that prior to coming here a few days ago you hadn't seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you showed it to me in your office the first time ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you look at the first name on that list.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zarko Cosic. I know him. We went to school together. In elementary school and then for a while the secondary school as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, it indicates on this list that he is the chief. You indicated at the beginning of your testimony that Dragan Veselic was the chief at one point. Do you know anything about what happened to Dragan Veselic?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, when I was released from Luka, between June and August, I was in Belgrade with my wife and I met a lot of Bosnian Muslims and Serb in Belgrade. There was a place in Belgrade where the locals of Brcko gathered and then I heard that Veselic had been killed in a traffic accident in Vojvodina, somewhere near Novi Sad. That's what I heard from the Serbs from Brcko and from the Bosnian Muslims from Brcko as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the individual at number 7, can you read out his name?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petar Pero Kaurinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And is this the Petar Kaurinovic who interrogated you at the Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And on the rest of that first part of the page, do you recognise any other names?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know most of these people. For example, number 4, Petar Gavrilovic, Dragica Tesic. Stojan Vasiljevic was my neighbour. Petar Stevic, I also know him from before the war. I know Cvetko. I know Ljubica Knezevic as well. Stevo Knezevic, who arrested him, is her brother. I also know Milenko Simikic [phoen], many others. Sojka Pajic, I also know her. She still works at the Brcko SUP in the office for the issuance of identity cards. I also know Branko Kisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we flip to page 5, please. Scroll up a little bit, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see the name at number 217?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Branko Pudic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned that Branko Pudic is the policeman who you saw on the first day who hit you on the back of the head; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes. Yes, that's him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we scroll down a little bit, please. A little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see the name at number 252?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Konstantin Simeunovic, aka Kole, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Is this the man who presented himself as the commander of the Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we flip to the next page, page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see number 297?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Dragan Zivkovic, also known as Travolta. Also a policeman before the war in Brcko, a professional policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see him during the month of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. On one occasion, before I was arrested, he came to my office in Elektro Company Brcko, together with Miso Cajevic. They both wore camouflage uniforms. They carried out interviews with every single employee. Before I was even arrested by those men and taken away, maybe two or three days before I was taken to Luka, that's when I met Dragan Zivkovic and Miso Cajevic in our company, on the premises of Elektrodistribucija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we scroll down a little bit more on that page?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you see the name at number 312?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Milomir Marinkovic. I believe that that's actually Mika. I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just to refresh our memories, who was Mika Marinkovic?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, he was issuing driving licences at the Brcko SUP. He was the secretary of the SUP. And during the war, I saw him in that Bimeks car that was passing by the Elektrodistribucija building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the Bimeks car, can you clarify the word "car" here. I'm sorry, it translated at the Bimeks car?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bimeks is actually a small lorry, and Bimeks was the company for the processing of meat and meat products before the war. And they used that small-tonne freezer lorry to transport their products, and it was painted white. And I don't know what it was used for during the war. I can only guess that it was used to transport dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this is the truck that you saw passing while you were working at the Elektro Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I realise that this is not a document that the witness can authenticate. He has been able to identify a number of policemen on this list. The document can be dealt with the next witness as well, so at this stage I would ask for it to at least be exhibited here, unless there's an objection from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we hear your objection, Mr. Cvijetic, counsel, could you assist us with the purpose for which this is being tendered? You will remember the -- this is a reminds -- a reminder of the path we took with -- I think it was the last document yesterday afternoon. The witness has spoken to such of it as a system, but again it isn't a document that he -- which he is the author and what does it do but add to the clutter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: At this stage, Your Honour, this is the type of document we would really insist to admit in evidence. It demonstrates the membership of certain individuals who were seen at the crime sites, members of the police. This is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, but the witness has testified to the presence and the actions of certain police officers whom he has identified. How does this advance the witness's testimony in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In the sense that he -- for example, Mr. Kaurinovic, who is number 7, on that day was wearing civilian clothes but know he was a member of the police. This document confirms it. I will not insist for this document to be exhibited. We can MFI it and let the next witness deal with it who was a member of the police. But this document demonstrates the membership of the police of certain perpetrators, and we believe that this goes to the linkage between the crimes and the accused in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It confirms that these persons were police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It confirms that these persons were police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Let me hear Mr. Cvijetic, please. I think he had a -- Mr. Cvijetic was it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't take up much of your time, Your Honours. I believe that the Prosecutor himself mentioned reasons for which this document cannot be admitted immediately. As for MFIing this document, we don't object because after this witness we will have another one who will be able to tell us more about the document, as well as about the names of the MUP members. So the witness that we are -- we have before us today is not the best suited to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So it makes life simple for everybody including the Chamber if it's marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P139, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P139, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, I'm going to jump a little bit in time. On the 7th of June, this is the day that you were released, you told us in the Krajisnik case, and this is at page 490 of the transcript, that a JNA captain by the name of Rade Bosic came and you described your exchange with him. You told us that you were taken to Kosta's office to have this discussion with Mr. Bosic. Can you tell us, did Mr. Kosta Simeunovic, did he have a permanent office at the camp, was there an office where he was regularly at?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. That building where they were, his office was somewhere in the middle. As you are looking at the building from the hangar, you will see that it has four entrances, and I believe that the middle entrance was the one leading to Kosta's office. That's the office that I went to when Rade came down there for the first time to inquire about me. And that's where I was with Kosta as well as with Goran Jelisic on that night. That was one and the same office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I will not ask you about the details of the exchange because you deal with it in the transcripts in the Krajisnik case. However, when you left the office, did you notice something on the door of that office?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only then, but also when I complained about the stomach pain, as I was leaving his office, there was a piece of paper on which Kosta wrote down and signed it in his own hand that nobody had a right to enter the hangar without his presence, that nobody had the right to ill treat and kill prisoners in the presence of other prisoners or without his supervision. This is roughly what I could read on that piece of paper. There was no stamp that I could see, but it was signed by Konstantin Simeunovic, Kole, as the deputy commander of the investigating camp Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this was on the door of his office?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned to us Goran Jelisic earlier. Can you tell us approximately how many times did you see him at the Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice in the hangar and the third time in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And it is correct to say that you didn't see Goran Jelisic killing anyone at the Luka camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, he did not kill anybody with me being present or seeing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And at page 459 of your Krajisnik testimony, you do say that you were told by other prisoners that they had seen Goran Jelisic kill prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard from two men who had been my colleagues. One was Smail Delic, and the other was Osman Stranjac. And his father also told me about an incident where he lay people down in front of the office building and shot in their heads. And during that incident, he killed maybe three or four men. All the three of them told me the same story. Osman Stranjac and Ahved Stranjac [phoen] themselves participated in the loading of bodies at the beginning of May 1992. Some 80 men Osman counted and they had to load them on to a military truck, and I don't know where the bodies were taken. In any case, he said that he was counting 80 dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I realise that you have called Mr. Gasi as a 92 ter witness, and you had indicated that you would spend one hour leading him through his previous testimonies. You've already spent an hour -- almost an hour and a half now, and it seems to me that what you have done actually is to examine him in chief as if he were a viva voce witness, which is kind of inappropriate when you have announced that he is to be called as a 92 ter witness. So I think in keeping in with your own identification of Mr. Gasi as a 92 ter witness, you are required to round up your introduction of this witness very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will deal with two other areas that were not covered in the Krajisnik case and we'll wrap up within the next 10, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please do so very briefly and very shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please do so very shortly and very briefly, and for the future, I think that we should stick to the main rule which has been explained in the procedural guide-lines that for 92 ter witnesses, 20 to 30 minutes will be the normal length of time to be used for introduction of the witness before we pass the floor on to the Defence counsels for cross-examination. So make up your mind as to how you wish to present the evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Your Honours. Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, you were mentioning in your Krajisnik evidence that at one point a man by the name of Vojkan Djurkovic visited the Luka camp. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vojkan Djurkovic came to the hangar twice or thrice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You also said in the Krajisnik case that on a number of times he visited, he addressed the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown a video, 65 ter 2108. It is a BBC programme called "Cracks in the Armour" from 1994. If we can show the first extract of that video, please. 2108. Yes, I need to say that this is in Sanction actually, the video. There seems to be a technical problem, Your Honours. This is the last part of my presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you move on to something else in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In the meantime, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, one other area that you did testify about in the Krajisnik case was the time you were taken to the police station to clean out the SJB. Do you remember that?
