utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Perhaps it was early June. The 1st of June or the 30th of May. I cannot recall exactly. Some people arrived from the police station asking for volunteers. They took some 15 people with them --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I don't want us to go into the details. I just want to confirm that you did see this event at the police station where you were taken and you witnessed the killing of two prisoners, and this was by a policeman in a blue uniform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I believe the video is available now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you see the video on the screen? The image?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can the first clip be played, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, do you recognise the man in this video, the man with the sunglasses?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May 1992 he looked somewhat differently. He used to wear a uniform, a camouflage uniform with the insignia of a major. And instead of boots, he had Adidas track shoes. But yes, this is Vojkan Djurkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This is the man that you describe as coming to the Luka camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we show the next clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you heard Mr. Djurkovic speak here. Is this the type of the speeches he would make at the Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he came to the Luka camp, he usually went to the middle of the hangar by himself. That was rather interesting to see. Then some of the prisoners recognised him. He told them, Come closer so that we can talk. And on one such occasion, I came close as well. We made a circle around him, and then he held speeches. There were two brothers from Brezovo Polje, whose names I cannot recall, and he seemed to have addressed them directly, and he told them, You remember when the Luka camp was opened and how things used to be here. I was trying to save people and I did. This was madness here. So you should tell about it. And then he would change his tone somewhat by saying things would be normalised here, conditions improved, and all will be well. I heard that some people consider me a war criminal. Whenever he came there, and I saw him on two or three occasions, he would hold -- give such speeches. Once he would leave, some half an hour later or 40 minutes later, four, five or six men in camouflage uniforms would burst in with shovels, starting to hit whoever they could in the hangar. Once done, they would leave and then the same people would come back bringing in coffee, as they say, to us, the Turks, the balijas, to have some to drink. Those same people who hit us with their feet and shovels, wanted to drink coffee with the same people they had previously beaten, and share their cigarettes with. That is what things were like in the Luka camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we show the third clip from this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, on this last clip he says that he should receive the Nobel Peace Prize and that people are free to return. What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was typical of such a person. As I used to know him in 1992. Who can say such things when the war in Bosnia was such a horrific event. I see it completely differently and I simply fail to understand this. I don't know. Madness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I will conclude my examination with this last clip, Your Honours. Can we show from this video the last clip, yes, fourth clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we freeze here for a second?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this individual?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Who is this?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we continue playing, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know who he is. Zarko Cosic. He is a lot fatter here, that is why I could not recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you continue playing, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, this is the new SJB chief in 1992, Zarko Cosic, who said that the conditions in Brcko were so difficult that they had to throw the Muslims out. Can you comment on this? Was the situation in Brcko so difficult?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why they had to throw me out of Brcko. Why was I taken away? Why was I held at the Luka camp? I did not present a problem. There was no reason for me to drive me out or to drive my father, brother, and sisters out. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I ask for this video to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Before I conclude, Your Honours, in relation -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Apologies. As Exhibit P139 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In relation to the newspaper article that was shown yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Item 139 was the list of policemen that was MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This will be Exhibit P140.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before I conclude, the newspaper article that we displayed yesterday and that Your Honours decided not to admit, I would ask -- it's 65 ter 267. Thank you. I do understand that this witness could not tender this document. Could I ask for it to be MFI'd for the time being with the possibility that somebody else may talk about it and authenticate the document. One clarification is I remember Your Honours saying yesterday that we don't have the source or the author, and I do apologise, last week we did realise that the translation we had and the original we had didn't have the source, but in the meantime by the end of the week we were able to locate the original. It was disclosed to the Defence and it shows that it was the newspaper "Oslobodjenje". So for the time being, if it could be marked and we'll see if another witness can talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's a matter on which we've ruled. We aren't going to revisit that. If another witness is able to prove it, we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just for the record, I was thinking if ever it is admitted, it would be good to know that this witness also talked about it. It's just for matters of record for final briefs or any other submissions in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I have no doubt the Prosecution in their closing submissions, that they would not fail to remind the Chamber of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Gasi.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm co-counsel in the team of Mr. Stanisic. I'll have a few questions of you. First, I'd like to deal with your membership in the SDA party. You were a member of the party; correct?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It says here between the 26th of May, 1990, until November 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic should make pauses between questions and answers. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. I apologise, can we have the page reference number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking the witness directly about his membership in the party. In his earlier interviews he mentioned that fact and I don't think that is in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise, because it says "it says here," I thought you were referring to the Krajisnik testimony. If that is not the case, that's perfectly fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, I will remind you -- I don't know if you heard the interpreter's intervention, but I would remind you of the need to slow down and allow time between the question and the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, obviously this is not in dispute and there is no need for me to jog your memory in terms of your previous testimonies.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any way you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: How did you see this party of yours, in one or two sentences?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first I believed it was supposed to be the party of all those people who were in favour of cohabitation in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let's try to define it then. The party that demanded that all peoples enjoy the same rights; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This opinion of yours about the party platform, did it remain the same or did you change it at some point?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It remained the same until I began attending Executive Board sessions in which I saw some people approach matters in a rather religious way, which I found a bit distasteful. I'm talking about the people at the local level. I have been an atheist throughout my life. I'm a former communist and this is what repelled me. It drove me away from the party. Of course to repeat, this is at the local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Concerning the party programme, it was supposed to be a party that would seek equal rights for the people of all three ethnicities. This included the right of every people to decide on their own fate, let's put it that way?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And say the Serb people could not dictate to the Muslims what sort of a state they would live in, whether they would live in Yugoslavia or in a separate sovereign state?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then you will agree that neither the Muslims nor the Croats could impose the same on the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by imposing, but if this is physical duress that we are talking about, then I wouldn't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No, that's not what I meant. I meant by out-voting the other two peoples --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm being told that it's time for the break, Your Honours? No? Oh, I need to go more slowly. I misunderstood my colleague. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So we agree, then. The Serbs could not force the Muslims or Croats and the other way around, to force this important issue on other peoples as to what kind of a state they would like to live in. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. Of course, no one can force anyone else to do something they don't want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, please wait before answering and I'm being criticised as well. We speak the same language.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we start to chat and then the interpreters are in trouble. Let's try and interpret the decision of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the 15th and 16th of October, 1991, by virtue of which it was decided on the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina without the approval and presence of Serb deputies, or of the SDS, so to say. I won't ask you about the constitutionality of that decision because you are not a constitutional expert, but such a decision, be it that included the imposition I have mentioned or anything else, goes to the crux of the matter.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, if you link the entire Serbian people to only one party, the SDS, then you are greatly mistaken. I think many Serbs did vote for them, but a great many of them were members of the SDP and other parties, such as Ante Markovic's party, and Bogic Bogicevic himself was a Serb who was a member of the Presidency of the SFRY at the time. If there is one party, as you yourself said, I'm not a constitutional expert, but if a party walks out of the parliament and still the parliamentary majority makes a decision, then it's a legitimate majority, a legitimate decision. Well, there may be various interpretations but this is how I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is what I'm discussing. It was not a legitimate majority because there was no required majority under the constitution. Making decisions that are of vital interest could not be even done by outvoting or simple majority, but by consensus and mutual agreement alone. You know that nowadays in the B&H parliament there is the House of the Peoples in which decisions are made by consensus and all the three peoples are on an equal footing. Mr. Gasi, if you feel incompetent to deal with this matter, just tell me and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, I have my opinion. You are probably more educated in the sense of law than me, but I may have a differing opinion about the legitimacy of the Serb deputies walking out and not participating in the referendum on independence. As a person, I never wanted to impose my opinion on anyone else or did I ever have anything against any single Serb in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I still don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll try to address you as a simple man. If three peoples cannot reach a consensus as to what type of state they would live in, what is an alternative to that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, and as our people would say, if a marriage is broke, it's broke. Split it. What was Bosnia like before the war? A journalist said that it resembled the patterns of a leopard skin. There were so many different peoples living in different people [as interpreted] and all of a sudden it was gone. It was gone from Brcko too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. If in that, as you called it, the divorce of three peoples in a peaceful way has as its only alternative war, and I consider them going their own ways bad too, isn't that the lesser evil than war?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived for 33 years in the former Yugoslavia, but I would have prayed to God even though I was -- had no religious affiliation for that country to be preserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You were a sportsman. How far did you get in sports?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990, I represented Yugoslavia at the world championship in Copenhagen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But you are saying as far as you are concerned, you think that it would have been a good thing for Yugoslavia to have been preserved?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So what was bad about the efforts of the Serbian people to preserve Yugoslavia and for the Serbs to stay within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened in Brcko was bad and what happened to me personally was bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No, we'll get to that yet.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat, please. I didn't get the essence of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll simplify. I will not go back to your opinion on Yugoslavia. But what would have been bad about the efforts of the Serbian people who, at their own referendum, stated that they wanted to remain in Yugoslavia and that they wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina to stay within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see nothing bad about the democratic vote of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, I agree with you when you said that the way -- I believe it was Ristanic drew that map about the -- about the division of Brcko wasn't good.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't only him. It was the entire SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, the way they went about it was inadequate clearly. It won't do to start constructing Berlin walls. But we see that the Dayton Accord actually resulted in -- had the same result, and there is even an unofficial entity called the Herceg-Bosna where the Croats are the majority; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know all that. I read the papers and I sometimes look at websites on the internet. I can tell you the Dayton Accord, to my mind, had as its purpose to stop the war and the killing and the destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. But that is what it achieved, peace was brought about by dividing the peoples along ethnic lines mostly. I agree with you that it shouldn't have been done in an absolute sense because Bosnia-Herzegovina can never be divided that way.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, Mr. Cvijetic, the way I was brought up it is clear to me that people cannot be divided by any borders. It's the politicians who divide them, the ideologists. If I start feeling threatened as a member of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it isn't my personal feeling; it's because I listen to my leaders. People listen to their leaders, that's why.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Gasi, I won't venture into politics and probably won't be allowed to go beyond what you have stated in the examination-in-chief. But let's go back to the events in Brcko. After the incidents in Bijeljina, did certain forces of the Muslim people of the SDA party started assembling with the intention to go to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Didn't you mention that Mr. Ramic intervened to that effect?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that a column of refugees from Bosanski Brod passed through Brcko after the crime at Sijekovac where the Croatian forces committed a crime on the Serb people. Did you witness that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We have mentioned the map drawn by Ristanic. I remember what you marked on the map as his marking. What is the name of that part of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was explaining that yesterday. These are the local communities leaning on the southeastern part of the town of Brcko. From the Serbian border, Stolina -- road to Bijeljina, Brcica and the town centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Isn't the majority of that part of town called Srpska Varos?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there has always been an Orthodox church there. It's still standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So that line of his mostly includes that part of town?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, when you left Brcko and when you were able to go abroad, you gave a statement to the Helsinki Committee? You remember probably.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It was in Denmark, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In that statement, you said, among other things, that the worst crimes in Brcko were committed by paramilitary formations. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You furthermore said that the most significant paramilitary group were the Arkan people and that they were led by someone from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that. I tried to correct that statement of mine but I never got the chance to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll go through that quickly. Then I suppose that you don't know that Zdravko Ljubinkovic?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any connection with that man whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then you allegedly said that both groups were united into the Serbian guards, both the Mauzer's guard and the Arkan -- Arkan's group led by Mirko Ilinkovic [as interpreted] were united?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they united later during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But did you know it at the time or did you say that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just said, I did give statements to the Helsinki Committee, but when I saw the document it was two or three months after -- or later. It was in English. I was never able to correct my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I remind counsel and the witness again to slow down. You are overlapping. And it's 12.05, so could we take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, I believe that we broke off when we spoke about the map drawn by Ristanic. You said in your earlier statement that you saw from your house that 300 to 400 people were killed in the town centre and that they were taken out in groups of 30 to 40, and that it took days to wash away the blood. Do you remember that part? It was put to you in your previous testimonies.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that Defence counsel did quote that statement to me that I gave to the Helsinki Committee and I said before that I never said that. Who in his right mind could say that 300 people were killed in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then you are saying that that is false?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: A photograph was shown to you, I believe it was a photograph with a Scorpion, and we are going to need it. In your statement you identified that person as Jovan Pudic. That is what the statement reads. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a copy from an English newspaper, I believe it was the Guardian. So the article was photocopied. And when we were discussing that photograph with a gentleman from the Helsinki Committee, I said to him that I was with the author of that photograph who had shown me other photographs where that man Pudic could be seen. But it was not that photograph. How that entered the report, I don't know because I didn't say it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you didn't identify that person as Jovan Pudic?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to -- I would like the photograph under 65 ter something but I believe it was 2164, I would like that photograph to be put up on the screen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That's the photograph. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The person carrying a Scorpion with a silencer, do tell me, you said that it was the policeman you had seen earlier, I believe that's what you said, in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which policeman?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you whether that was a policeman and whether you can compare him with the other whom you saw in the city?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I replied that it was not the same man.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I want to ask then whether that's a police officer?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is wearing a police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do tell me what you see, which parts of the police uniform you see?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Slow down. The interpreters can't follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, do wait after my question. Do look at that person and tell me what he is wearing, which parts of a police uniform, the ones that were used before the war, and you and I remember very well. Wait a minute. Now, tell us.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the blue short-sleeved shirt and the boots and the trousers he is wearing are police trousers. It's this dark shade of blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, before the war, the trousers were light coloured and they were wearing shoes rather than boots?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, but the police officers did wear boots too, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is anything missing on the shirt?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? What could be missing? It's a police shirt, short sleeved --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did they wear anything on their shoulders?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did wear a rank insignia, but it can't be seen in this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, it can't be seen because there aren't any. They would have been on his shoulders.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the way you look at it. I believe it's a police shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Uniform hat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic and Mr. Gasi, you have been reminded on several occasions today about the need to slow down so the interpreters can interpret what you are saying. This continuing "chat," to use your words, Mr. Cvijetic, may be useful to you but it isn't helpful to the interpreters. At the end of the day it doesn't assist the record. Please discipline yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we have reached a stage when you could probably punish me and it may even be efficient. Of course that's joke.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, speaking about uniforms, you said today that Ranko Cesic also wore police uniform and that Goran Jelisic did and also the person you identified as Jovan Pudic, that he was a police officer. You said that -- help me with the last name, please, and you say you know him, Konstantin Simeunovic, also know as Kole. Is that his name?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Kosta Simeunovic, Konstantin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: He also wore a police uniform?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll have to return to the list of police officers, if you will just let me find that Prosecution exhibit which was shown to the witness. You recognised Branko Pudic on that list. The name was shown to you and you recognised Branko Pudic. Just give me a minute to find the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was shown as a 65 ter exhibit. Let us just see the page number. Yes. Under 65 ter it was 2138, so let us immediately go to page 5. Page 5 in B/C/S, please. That's number 5, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Look at the part that is being shown to you, that is being blown up for you. Under 212, Pero Pudic, am I right?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let's move on. Under 217, Branko Pudic?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Under 222, Boro Pudic?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In your statement, Jovan Pudic?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The Helsinki Committee?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this, to this very day, okay, today I'm sure what Pudic's name was, the one who hit me. Every time, including that statement that I provided to the Helsinki Watch Committee, that was the one and the same Pudic that I saw. And I don't know how the name Jovan entered that report. I never said the whole name because I didn't know. And I know Pudic because I've known him from before the war and that's the Pudic that I have in mind, Branko Pudic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the same list can we go to number 252, please. And let's find the person under that number. The policeman under 252, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Look at the list. It says Simonovic, Konstantin. Do you allow for the possibility that that is not the person called Konstantin Simeunovic?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my mistake. I believe very probably that his same is Simeunovic. I apologise but I know Kosta really very well and that's Kosta, Konstantin Simeunovic, that's the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Again you say Simeunovic?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the way I'm saying. It could be Simonovic, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But you are correcting yourself when I show the name to you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are absolutely right but that's the same person. It's the same Kosta, the same Kole that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I can't agree with you. He can't be the same. There's no other way to identify him. Maybe a photo would help?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you do have a photo I'll be able to identify the man. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Gasi, I apologise, I just called you Mr. Pudic. In your earlier testimonies you put a military uniform on Cesic. You put a military uniform on Goran Jelisic as well. I have to face with you your previous statements provided in the previous cases that you testified in. The Krajisnik case, 4 February 2004. You were describing the moment when he arrived in the hangar. I'm referring to Goran Jelisic, of course. And you say this: "He came to the hangar. He was wearing a camouflage uniform of the JNA. I didn't see any markings or ranks. He did not wear a cap. "I'm asking you again, what kind of camouflage uniform was he wearing at the time? "As far as I'm familiar with uniforms, I believe that it was a camouflage JNA uniform?"

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is what I still claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Didn't you tell us that he arrived in a blue police shirt and that he was wearing the markings with the one star showing that he was an inspector?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was on another occasion when Kosta took me to the office and when we had a short discussion. That's when he was wearing a blue police uniform with one star showing that he was a senior police inspector. That's when he was wearing that uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You explained that that one star at that time as the rank of a lieutenant -- sergeant on his military camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must have made a mistake. I can't remember. But I know that Goran liked to change uniforms very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could hear from the Serbs in the hangar and the guards, the more valuable a uniform was perceived the more prone he was to wearing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And on those uniforms that he wore, did he add ranks to the uniform?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, it is possible. Just like Major Duskanovic did. I can't believe that that person could have ever reached the rank of a major before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could Goran Jelisic be a member of the police in the first place?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Based on what?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he wore the uniform when I saw him wearing that uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You've just told us that he was wearing both the police and the military uniform at the same time. Could he be both a policeman and a member of the military?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, I'm sure that you know it only too well who was distributing uniforms at the time to the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and what the role of Jelisic was at that time when he wore one kind of uniform and what was the role of Mr. Jelisic when he wore the other kind of uniform, I really can't talk about that. But I can easily assume that he was a member of the army for awhile and then a member of the police, and I'm basing that assumption on the basis of the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Only on the basis of the uniform?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is there a possibility that members of the paramilitary formations also came by those uniforms and that they changed them at their own will?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that they did. I'm sure that you are right. I would agree with you in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me quote from your statement, or rather, your testimony from another case, or rather, it was still the same case, the Krajisnik case. Page 456 starting with line 4: "Ranko Cesic would come wearing a JNA uniform." And so on and so forth. So there you have Ranko Cesic in a military uniform, and today you told us he was wearing a police uniform?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that before and today.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Why are you changing your testimony, Mr. Gasi?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not changing my testimony, Mr. Cvijetic. When people ask me, I tell them what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, you testified in the Milosevic case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic was charged with responsibility for the participation of JNA units in the events in Brcko and you will remember that at the time the Prosecutor and Milosevic himself asked you a lot about the role of the JNA in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It was interesting at the time to prove that members of the paramilitary formations actually belonged to the JNA. And you, on page 75, line 24 and 25 in that case, said that Ranko Cesic was a member of the JNA. Who else could he have belonged to? He was wearing a camouflage JNA uniform?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what is in dispute here?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And now you are telling us, or rather, you told us then, who else could he belong to? Today, earlier today, you said that he wore a police uniform.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the Prosecutor asked me, and I told him that I also saw him wearing a police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Cvijetic, if it's possible to give us the exact page number in the Milosevic case. Because you said page 75, but we have the sequential number is actually in the 26.000's, so if you could give us that page number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milosevic, I have a print-out of the transcript in English so we can actually check the page number that I'm quoting. Page 75. Date, 21 October 2009. Well, no, no, that's when this was printed. It's page 75, lines 24 and 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It appears that you have printed it off the version that doesn't have a sequential number. Because the page number where his testimony starts at is 26.430.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. My apologies. You are absolutely right. 26.449 is what has been printed. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, I was looking at the page markings. So yes, indeed, we are on that same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Where you said, and there's no two ways about it that he was a member of the JNA, not for a single second in any of the previous testimonies did you say that he was wearing a police uniform. Please hold on just for a moment. The Milosevic case, the Krajisnik case, the Tadic case, three cases, and in all the three you said that Cesic wore a military uniform, and the first time today you mentioned that he wear a police uniform. And today, people on trial are heads of the police. Doesn't this look suspicious to you, Mr. Gasi?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, Mr. Cvijetic, you know very well who dressed people in uniforms in the former Yugoslavia, and I'm telling you what I saw at the time. I'm not putting any uniforms on anybody. I just said that he wore two different kinds of uniforms. Who Ranko Cesic belonged to, I believe and I know that before the war started in Brcko Mr. Cesic wore a camouflage uniform around Brcko, and that he was a member of the special units of the JNA. I don't know whether his role changed during the war. In any case, he also appeared in the police uniform when he came to look. That's all I know. I'm not putting anything on anybody, and I never said that I put a JNA uniform on anybody. That was the uniform that he wore and I assume that it was a JNA uniform. That's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Mr. Gasi, I have to confront you with your own testimonies. Krajisnik, 4 February 2004, page 406. Again Cesic, a soldier wearing a military uniform. No police uniform in sight. Page lines 17 to 29. I have to tell you that I don't know what to choose from which case, to be honest, but what I have to tell you is the fact that we haven't been able to find anywhere that you say that those people were wearing police uniforms. It was only today that you mentioned it for the first time ever.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've tried to answer. I've tried to tell you what I think and what I know. And it's up to you. I did not have any intention to put any uniforms on anybody in order to reflect the nature of any of the cases. That's my opinion, and if I'm mistaken, I apologise if I put a uniform on somebody that he never wore. But I'm sure that I didn't make a mistake because I'm telling you what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, we still have the impression that you are adapting your testimony to the accused.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please allow me to finish. If it was interesting to put military uniforms on them in the Milosevic case, then you put military uniforms on them. If the accused are people in charge of the police, then you put police uniforms on them. That's the long and the short of it. Let me go back to the case of Dusko Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'm going to give you the transcript page. The date is 15 May 1996. And the page number is 739, lines 11 to 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Here you say about Goran Jelisic that he put the star on the military camouflage uniform and that he liked to be exclusively dressed, that he liked to wear a special uniform and that the rank that he wore was the rank of a corporal. Today you are saying that the star was the star featuring on the uniform of a police inspector. Do you know that that star does not exist in the police and that it doesn't stand for a police inspector in the police?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I don't understand you. I'm not an expert. I'm just telling you what I thought at the time. Before the war, police inspectors had stars. If your information tells you differently, then I don't know. I'm not an expert. I'm not a big expert. I can't tell you what position people held.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to try to assist you with that. In the police there are functions. The function of a police inspector and so on and so forth, there are no ranks at the moment. So how may we account for your behaviour today?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing to explain. I'm telling you what I saw. I don't see a reason for any doubts. What is disputable about uniforms? I'm not here to put uniforms on people. I'm telling you what I saw and I'm talking about the types of uniforms that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The Krajisnik case, 4 February 2004, page 456, lines 1 to 5. Ranko Cesic came in an olive-drab JNA uniform. That's what you said, and I must admit, I don't know how many times do I have to show you all that, I am not convinced in the authenticity of your words.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very sorry that you did not get from me what you wanted. I'm just telling you what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise, but I think the witness has answered enough on this question and he's said repeatedly that Jelisic and Cesic liked to change their uniforms. What else is counsel trying to get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Cvijetic, Mr. Cvijetic, can I just ask you just for clarification that the photos we saw, which were exhibited as P133 and P134, I believe those photos were of Mr. Jelisic, were they not, and there apparently he was dressed in a blue shirt at least, which would indicate a police uniform. Or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really don't know who is depicted in that photo. Far be it from me to try and identify the people in the photo. But let me remind you that in the Jelisic case it was established that he was never a member of the police force. If nothing else, we can claim that with certainty, and please don't ask me about the photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: As we are speak being that photo, I would like to have that photo on the screen again, if possible. I think it's P132 or P133. 133, sorry. That was the previous one. Yes, that's the one. Could we zoom in on the right hip of the man dressed in the blue shirt. Just a moment, I have to take the other one. More, please. Yes. Can the witness tell us what he sees on the belt of the man? Eventually we zoom in a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a police baton that used to be used before the war, and I still think they have the same ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, while we're on this photograph, this cowboy style wearing of a uniform, do you believe it is appropriate of a police member?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before the war. That far you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gasi, at Luka, as you said, when that lieutenant came, he ordered Kole to bring you in; am I correct? Did I understand correctly, the JNA lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not clear about this. To bring me where?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The one that set you free from the Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Bosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: He ordered that you be taken out?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he came to fetch me from the hangar. He brought me outside and told me we are going on a trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Was there a lieutenant inside of the JNA, I think you mentioned him when Jelisic came?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a lieutenant. There was a JNA major that was there on one occasion, escorted by two policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What did he order?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked who we are and where the Muslim snipers are, and then Kosta indicated two men who were lying on the ground to my right. Then the major approached him, escorted by the two policemen and began interrogating them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your testimony today you were shown a video-clip with Vojislav Djurkovic, who, as you say, was a major since he sported that rank but he wore running shoes?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You say that the other prisoners in the camp told you that he behaved well towards them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My last question to you is, Mr. Gasi, when Kole took you out and he told you that you were to go home, he said again you will row on the Yugoslav team; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Would you have been glad to have been able to compete for Yugoslavia again?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm glad to hear that and I see a tear in your eye which tells me that you are being sincere. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If the witness needs time to recompose before we move on, then let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have cross-examination for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just a couple of issues, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: At page 48/25, of today's transcript, Mr. Cvijetic asked you when was your membership to the SDA. I think there was a little error in the transcript it said 26th of May, 1990, to November 1992. Is there an error in that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: November 1992 may be a mistake. I apologise. I wasn't focused enough. Me leaving the SDA and the Executive Council happened before the first multiparty elections in Bosnia. I did not wish to be put on a list. I'm not sure whether it was in November, but in any case, it was before the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: During the time of your detention at the Luka camp, were you a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps not a member, but a sympathiser.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could I have P129 again on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: At page 55/19 of today's transcript, Mr. Cvijetic asked you about the map that Mr. Ristanic was drawing, or at least that the SDS had provided, and he asked you about the area called Srpska Varos. If we look at the first page of P129, the first paragraph deals with the percentages in the Brcko municipality. And the last sentence, if you see the last sentence, it says that 41.346 people were registered in the town, among whom 20 per cent were Serb, 6.9 per cent were Croat, 55.8 per cent were Muslims. Does that agree with your recollection of the ethnic breakdown in the town of Brcko at that time?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The last topic that I'd like to cover is this issue of the uniforms of Mr. Cesic and Mr. Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The same document at page 3 of the English version. I'll try to find the equivalent in the B/C/S version. That is page 4, the bottom of that page in B/C/S, the page which has 4 on the top actually. If it's easier I'll say the ERN. It's 0074-1400 on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: While that document is being brought up, Mr. Gasi, do you remember earlier today you told us that a number of people were in the police intervention platoon, and you also stated that Mr. Cesic was a member of the police intervention platoon. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The last paragraph of that document in the B/C/S and at page 3 is the paragraph before the last. In the middle of that paragraph, doesn't it say that there was a number of paramilitary troops in that area and that when the war started and during the combat activities, a number of members of these units joined the police intervention platoon. Isn't that what it says?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And my last question, on those photos, earlier today I asked you if you recognise -- if the policeman on those photos was the same as the one you saw on the 7th of May. You told us this was not the same man. But on those photos, were you able to recognise who that man was? Once you saw the photos.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I never even said I could recognise him on a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. I apologise, Your Honours, one last question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Counsel said to you today that on a number of occasions in the Tadic case, the Milosevic case and the Krajisnik case, you said that Cesic and Jelisic were wearing camouflage uniform. Do you remember having given a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1995 to Mr. Buckley and Madam Castro?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And could in the English version page 9 be displayed? In Sanction, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The third line deals with Goran Jelisic. Doesn't it say there that he was "keen on changing his uniform"?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And does that recollect with your memory?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, we thank you for coming to testify once again before this Tribunal. We wish you a -- you are now released and we wish you a safe journey back to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, the Prosecution is ready to call its next witness, Mr. Ignjic, and I now call that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please make your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you give us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Cvjetko Ignjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a machinist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And could you tell us when and where you were born, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 25th of December, 1948, in Covic Polje, the municipality of Orasje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you given testimony previously before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In addition to those personal details that the President just obtained from you, can you tell us if these details are correct: Although born in Orasje, you've lived most of your life in Brcko municipality or in the town of Brcko; is that correct? And don't just nod, always answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the town of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1972, you joined the police and thereafter you had a career in the police as a police crime scene technician?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You continued working in the police until 1993, when you retired but nonetheless continued doing police work as part of your wartime obligation?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: As part of your duties as a crime scene technician, did that involve examining the scenes of crimes and gathering and recording whatever evidence you could find there, such as photographs, finger-prints, and other similar tasks?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And I think you examined during the course of your career about 5.000 crime scenes of which about a thousand were murders. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Just turn your attention now to the events in Brcko in late April -- or in April and May of 1992. During that period of time were you married?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the month of April, did you take your wife anywhere?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Just before the beginning of May, I took her to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And can you explain what your reason was for doing that?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Everyone expected there would be a war and one could feel tension in the air. I was afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Although there was an expectation of war and tension in the air, had hostilities actually broken out in Brcko or in the Brcko municipality?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: The war began precisely on the 1st of May in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what, to your mind, was the event that symbolises or marks the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I think that it was the shooting in the eastern part of Brcko, between Grtica [phoen] and Begovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What shooting are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: One could actually hear detonations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's actually part of the township of Brcko itself. Do I understand you correctly or not?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want you to briefly look at a document that I produce to you. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown 65 ter 92. And for the benefit of the court ushers, on the B/C/S version that I want to show to the witness, the section is actually on the fourth -- third page of the document and it's self-evident that it's the section there headed "Brcko." And if we could also have the English, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, this document is a document that predates the commencement of war in Brcko, according to your calculations. It's dated 21 April 1992. And it's apparently directed to the minister of the interior and signed by the gentleman named, and you can see that on the B/C/S version, a gentleman named Predrag --

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Predrag Jesuric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: -- Jesuric. That's right. Did you know him during the war?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Had you heard of him as the CSB chief in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The section on Brcko which I think you can read, I hope you can read, in that particular document.

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: No, no, I understand that. I know you are not the author of the document, but I just want to ask you some questions about the content. The author of the document, this Predrag Jesuric, in speaking about Brcko, says that he is getting information on Brcko Serbian municipality from JNA colleagues with whom the Bijeljina CSB chief has contacts. And goes on to say that there are no combat activities in the area. As far as you are aware, thinking about your experience in the police force, were you aware of the JNA providing intelligence or information to CSB chiefs? Did that ever occur during the period of time that you were in the police, that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the relationship between the police and the army and what sort of communication they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The document itself goes on to refer in the very last couple of sentences or last sentence, in fact, that: "Meetings with SJB chiefs are to be organised, as well as chiefs of stations, that are to be set up in the Serbian municipalities of Zvornik and Brcko, that will eventually belong to Bijeljina CSB." In April of 1992, were you aware of any Serbian municipalities to be established in Zvornik and Brcko?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In April of 1992, can you remember who the chief of police was in Brcko itself, and his ethnicity? If you can't remember his name, at least try and give us the ethnicity of the gentleman?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: He was definitely a Croat, a Catholic. I think his name was Mijo, but I'm not sure. The HDZ delegated him according to the party key and he was appointed the chief of SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some more details about events in early May, but by early May of 1992, in Brcko, was there another chief of police; and if so, what was that person's name?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I'd seek to tender that document into evidence or at least have it marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: To what end is this being tendered? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, the document itself is relevant to JCE issues, communications between the military and the police, and it's also relevant to the establishment of the Serbian municipalities in Brcko. And it also goes to establish what the state of play was in Brcko municipality at the time prior to the outbreak of war in 1992. In May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But how does it come through this witness? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, that is why I said if the Trial Chamber is not disposed to admitting the document, that it be marked for identification at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Di Fazio, what exactly is the document? I -- MR. DI FAZIO: It's not headed by any -- it's not headed by any -- it's not headed as a decision. It's obviously a letter or a communication directed to the minister or deputy minister of the interior, and from a police chief, CSB regional police chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In Bijeljina. MR. DI FAZIO: He is based in Bijeljina. The author of the document is Mr. Jesuric. And the intended recipient is the Ministry of the Interior, attention for the minister or his deputy minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic is on his feet, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you anticipated the essence of my objection. We cannot even mark this document for identification through this witness because he doesn't know anything about the document. And you can see what the document is like. It would be appropriate to tender it when we have witnesses who belong to the police who may know something about this. But this witness explicitly stated he knew nothing about this document. MR. DI FAZIO: If I can say, just comment on that. This is most definitely a document that should be marked for identification if Your Honours are against me on admitting fully the document into evidence. It's been referred to in the record. The only way to maintain and track the use of this document is precisely for it to be marked for identification. And if -- and it may then be admitted at a later stage after hearing further evidence from other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I'm not sure understand what you mean by should be marked for identification. I've heard what you said, but I confess, I don't follow the -- your reasoning. MR. DI FAZIO: My colleague from the Defence just objected to its even being marked for identification. I'm saying that if you don't -- if you are not with me on the full admission of the document into evidence, then at the very least it should be marked for identification so that at a later stage if there's further evidence about the document or its provenance, where it comes from, who wrote it, then at that point the document that is marked for identification can be fully admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we'll mark this for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P141, marked for identification, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, earlier in your testimony you mentioned to us that you had gone to Bijeljina and taken your wife there, I believe, for her safety. What did you do upon your return to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I went to my house, home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you go to the police station or report for duty upon your return from Bijeljina at all?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No, I believe it was a weekend. It was the 1st of May, so there were two work-free days. I believe that I went home without going to the station first.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you eventually go to the police station, and if so, how did that come about?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: When the declaration was published on Radio Brcko, it was called Serbian Radio Brcko then, calling upon all of us to report to the stations, I went there. It was on the 1st of May in the early evening hours, or the late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was that essentially a mobilisation call? Some sort of mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And is that the central police station in Brcko itself?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you see police officers present?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you see any other persons or people apart from police officers inside the police station or around the police station?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were some troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And can you describe them, please? Can you describe the uniforms they were wearing and their ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: They were mostly unknown to me. They wore -- some wore camouflage uniforms, others wore old military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And ethnicity, please? What sort of -- where were they from?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I didn't really know. They were mostly unknown people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were they Croats?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No. I think they were Serbs but I don't really know. But I suppose they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: On that occasion when you first went back to the police station, did you find out what their business was, what they were doing there in the police station?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I learned that on the previous night they had liberated the SUP, that the chief had been replaced, and that there was now a new chief in place. And the police station had become the Serbian SUP or the Serbian police station, whichever way you want it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. The -- can you describe the atmosphere that was in the police station on this occasion. Was it a calm, orderly situation, or did it differ from that? Do your best and give the Trial Chamber an idea of what the atmosphere was like when you first went back and discovered all of this?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: It was rather awkward. All the office had been broken open. Things had been stolen from in there. There was shooting in town. There was chaos. It was a really war-like atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Does your description of chaos also describe to the police station?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No, I returned home in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How did you -- well, let me rephrase that. Did you go back to the police station over the next few days or not?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No, I went home and after four or five days, they came for me to report to the criminal police department saying that the Serbian police station had been established under Serbian criminal police and that I had to report for duty, and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Had you just taken the time off or did you get permission to go home for a few days?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No. On the 1st of May, when I went home in the evening, in that neighbourhood where my house is, the neighbours and I were on duty in one of the houses. But in that neighbourhood there was no fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Which neighbourhood of Brcko is that?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: The -- it was the Es neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was there fighting going on in Brcko town itself?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: In those early days, there was fighting around Izvori [phoen]. It's a part of town mostly populated by Muslims. And the very centre of town and the eastern parts of town, there was no fighting there. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I'd like to show the witness 65 ter 947, please. Both the English and the B/C/S, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: While that's coming up on the screen. I think you can already see the B/C/S. It's the second paragraph that I'm interested in. But firstly, the document itself, you can see that it's dated from the 6th of May, 1992. It's a Ministry of the Interior daily report signed on behalf of the minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic. And it refers to: "Ongoing fierce fighting in Brcko. According to the latest reports, the Serbian Territorial Units are on the offensive."

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's more or less how it was. There was fighting throughout May. There was fighting around Brcko practically throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And -- but was it fierce fighting at the time on the 6th of May, from what you recall, or was it just pockets of resistance around town? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I think that in the first two months there was fierce fighting daily. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I seek to tender or have this document marked for identification on precisely the same basis as the last document. I might add that this document and the previous document, of course, are either directed to one of the accused, Mr. Stanisic, or authored or signed on his behalf. In this particular case, the document is signed on behalf of Mr. Stanisic. The previous document, it was directed to him, addressed to him or to the ministry. But I just make clear that my application is to either admit the document, or if you are not with us, to at least have it marked for identification until there is later evidence in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my objection is identical as the previous one. My learned friend from the Prosecution has himself stated the reason why we cannot accept the admission of this document as evidence. As for marking it for identification, we are in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, could you -- [Microphone not activated] I'm not sure about to whom this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could you please clarify for us to whom this document is addressed. I see that it is signed by Mico Stanisic on behalf of the MUP in Sarajevo, but who is the addressee? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, it would appear to be at least a Ministry of the Interior document. It's a daily report. At the top left-hand corner of the document it says the ministry, and I dare say it's either -- I dare say that it's a document intended as an archival record for the Ministry of the Interior at least. Now, I can't tell from the face of the document whether it was ever intended that it should go beyond the Ministry of the Interior to other government organs or other government representatives. At this stage there's no evidence about that. But on the face of the document it just remains a daily report emanating from the ministry -- coming out of the Ministry of the Interior. I can't shed any light at this stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Di Fazio. That explains at least part of the reason why the Chamber is unable to admit it into evidence. So the maximum we can do is to MFI it. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I'm -- my conjecture has just been confirmed by my colleague Mr. Demirdjian. There will be evidence in this case showing that these documents were later sent to the government.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's admitted as Exhibit P142, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, you have something before we take the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we can clarify a misunderstanding. The signature on this document is not the signature of Mico Stanisic. The Prosecutor himself said that it was signed on behalf of Mico Stanisic which means that the document was signed by somebody else. That is all I wanted to clarify. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There's no dispute about that, yes. We return in 60 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honours, before witness is starting, just for the record, I'm back. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Adjusting parts of the mechanisms. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would remind the witness that he is still on his oath. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, thank you. Can the witness be shown MFI P139. That was the document marked earlier this morning during the Mr. Demirdjian's examination-in-chief of the former witness. MFI P139. It's a list of employees of the police. Can we get the English up as well or -- it's coming, is it? Thank you. We'll proceed with the B/C/S in the meantime because ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Firstly, that document, on the face of it, is dated 7 October 1992 and it purports to be a list of employees of the Brcko public security station for -- relating to salaries for the month of September 1992. At the top it says number 1, Zarko Cosic, chief, and you can take it from me that he has also signed and stamped the document. Who was Zarko Cosic?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of SUP in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know when he was appointed and how it came to be that he was appointed chief of police?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: The late Veselic got killed and he was chief before. I don't know when that happened. I can't remember. And I believe that Zarko Cosic came after him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. I don't think this is in dispute. Are you talking about a man named Dragan Veselic who was killed in a car accident in Serbia, and this fellow Cosic replaced him?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
