utterances.text: Thank you. Just cast your eye down the -- we have the English now. Cast your eye down the list of names on the first page and pay, of course, attention to number 13 and this appears to be your name. Are they all police officers whose names you see there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is -- we cannot interpret. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness, can I just interrupt you briefly. If you can just do it in silence, just cast your eye down, you don't have to read it out for us. And look down the first page and if you need to go any further, let us know. But that first page, are they all police officers?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Which one isn't a police officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Before you go any further, were they employees or working for and on behalf of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: They were employed by the SUP in order to make up the numbers since there were no Croats and Muslims available.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. So, for example, number 35, Trifka Zimonjic, the cleaning lady, she wasn't actually carrying out any police duties at all, other than cleaning the police station; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And of course number 13, Cvjetko Ignjic, described as forensic technician, that's a reference to you, is it not?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown the second page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Again, cast your eye down that list, and other than people who were written there in order to make up numbers, are the remainder police officers who were functioning and working at Brcko in 1992?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And just to wrap this up, some individual names, please. MR. DI FAZIO: If we could just scroll down to 100. I think that's on the -- must be the next page. 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Petar Djokic. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Before the war he graduated from the police school, then on the eve of the war he was a member of the municipal board as a politician, and later on, I don't know exactly when he became commander. He is a police officer by profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I now seek to tender that document fully into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P139 admitted in evidence, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I've finished with that document for the time being. Can we now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, before we leave the document, I wonder if it would make any sense to elicit from the witness if he can tell us about the ethnicity of the people on the list, because the document, as I recall, was from a later point, was it September or. MR. DI FAZIO: I can do that. I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Again while we've still got the document up there, all of the names that you've -- that I've directed your attention to so far in the last few minutes, all of the names that you've seen as you cast your eye up and down the list at least on the first two page, what ethnicity are the people whose names are written there?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I believe that a majority were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you see a single Croat or Muslim there anywhere?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No, not at the moment. No. MR. DI FAZIO: Does Your Honour wish me to take the matter any further than that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've mentioned that you got -- took your wife to Bijeljina, came back, took a few days off, and then went back to work and you described the scene that met you when you came back. Did you become aware of any killings, murders, killings that had occurred in the town of Brcko upon your return to the police station?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were colleagues of mine who worked with me even before the war and I heard from them. They told me everything that was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what did they say was happening in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: That there had been a lot of killed. Dragisa told me that there had been about 40 bodies discovered until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The man you just called Dragisa, is that Dragisa Tesic?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Dragisa Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And was he --

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the inspector. Yes, he was an inspector who worked with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you get any information as to the ethnicity of the people who had been killed?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: A rumour had it that most of them were Muslims. Those who had remained in the city. I'm not sure about every single of them, I'm not sure about a hundred per cent of them. But a majority of the cases involved Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, I don't think it's in dispute that in May of 1992 you performed some work at a grave-site. I want to ask you how it came to be that you came to be carrying out that work?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: When I was called to come to the SUP on the 5th or the 6th of May, I don't know when exactly, I don't know who it was who told me, either Dragisa or the chief that I was supposed to go to carry out identification of the bodies who were being buried. I was to replace Dragisa who was called to another place. Before I came, it was Dragisa who was doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. So you were tasked with carrying out this process of identification and it was an instruction that was given to you by police, either Dragisa or Veselic. Is it -- do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you told where to go, where to find this grave-site?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I believe that Dragisa showed it to me. It was a long time ago. It's very difficult for me to remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you eventually go out there and look at the location?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you got there, what did you first see? And I'm talking about the occasion when you first went to this place?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I saw the road towards Bijeljina, the road forked off on the right-hand side towards a farm, and on the right-hand side a hole had been dug out some 5 to 6 metres wide and some 10 to 15 metres long. It was about 3 metres deep, and at the bottom of that hole or pit I saw certain number of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was the -- is there a farm anywhere near the location?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did it have a name? If so, what?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: It was the so-called Bimeks farm. Bimeks was a meat processing company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And were you given any assistance by the police to carry out this process of identification or were you carrying out this task by yourself?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I was assisted by the workers from the utility company who brought the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But you were the only policeman operating and working at the site?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: The only forensic technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how the bodies got there?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: The utility company had a vehicle. It was a small cooler truck. That truck belonged to the utility company. In the course of the morning, they would go and collect bodies if they had learned -- if it had been reported to them that there were dead bodies to be found lying somewhere on the road. And they would bring such dead bodies close to the farm where they were deposited.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was there any heavy earth-moving equipment nearby during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I remember that there was a yellow excavator that does do some earth works, but I don't know exactly where it was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell the Trial Chamber how you came to go to the grave-site, this grave that had these people in it? Was it something that you did every day or something you were notified about or something done according to a schedule? How did you come to go -- actually go there?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: The workers from the utility company called a duty officer. The duty officer would tell me. I would get into my car and I would go there. I spent nights and days at the SUP building. I never went home. I slept there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But the instructions to go on any given day to the mass grave-site emanated, as far as you were concerned, from the duty officer, the police duty officer?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you recall how often you went to the site of the grave during the month of May?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: You can find the dates when I went there. I believe that it was more frequent in the month of May, and as time went on, it happened less frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about June and early July, did you also go to the grave-site?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: In early July. I believe that early July was the time when that grave-site was no longer used and was replaced by a normal procedure to bury dead bodies at regular cemeteries. I believe that -- actually, it was in early June when a more normal procedure was put in place to bury dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. And just to finally be clear on this issue of visits, you've talked about May and you've clarified the situation for early June -- for early July. In June, did you go to carry out the same sort of tasks at the grave-site?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understood your question properly. I did go there in the month of May and the month of June, and then in early July, dead bodies started being buried according to a normal procedure. In cases of crimes there were investigations. And I believe that already in the month of July there was a case of foul play and that that was investigated by the Brcko court. And that from then on, the procedure that was followed was a more normal, regular burial procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. I'd like to show you two photographs now. MR. DI FAZIO: The first one I'd like to show you is P135. Can that be put up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you recognise that location?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the grave-site.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: And can the witness be shown 65 ter 2692. Can that also be put up on the screen. Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment, please. That's not the photograph that I intended to exhibit. Would Your Honours just give me a moment, please. My apologies, my mistake. 2693. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise that --

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I don't have a photograph in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You will in a moment. Just hang on.

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Oh, it's the same photograph with a perhaps wider angle. MR. DI FAZIO: Would the ushers be so kind as to try and get a bigger image of the gentleman standing to the right of the photograph. You can see him there in what appears to be a brown jacket. That man. Thanks. Okay. That will be enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you recognise that individual?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Aco Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And who is Aco Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: He drove the truck. He was an old worker from Brcko. By that time he may have been 60 years old. He used to work for the public utility company, fixing their trucks and driving them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You've told us that the police provided you with information about where these bodies were coming from. Did you ever get information from the drivers of trucks, for example, from Mr. Stevanovic, as to where they were picking up and collecting bodies?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I never asked questions about that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You may not have asked questions but perhaps they might have volunteered information. Did they ever volunteer any information to you about where they were collecting these bodies that you, throughout the month of May and June, and early July of 1992, were burying in a pit? Did you ever ask them that question?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I may have but I can't recall any details now. I don't know. It was a long time ago. They probably did say things about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Would it assist you to refresh your memory, since you can't recall any details now, to look at a statement that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 29th of October, 2002, with a view to refreshing your memory? Would that be of assistance to you?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps. MR. DI FAZIO: I would like the witness to be -- would Your Honours just bear with me. Be shown on the screen 65 ter 10025. 10025.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, do you want that previous photo exhibited? MR. DI FAZIO: I do, and I'll just -- I'm going to come back to that so I will be asking for that one to be made a full exhibit. But in the meantime, if we could just deal with the topic of the memory. Thank you. And can we go to page 3. Yes, the third page in of the English. And I am afraid I don't know where it appears in the B/C/S because -- I'll do my best, but -- it's about -- the paragraph I'm interested in is about midway down in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Perhaps if just I read out the English paragraph to you, that will assist. Sorry, my apologies --

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: "The corpses were being collected in the towns and its environs. I never asked Stevanovic where he collected the bodies."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to read slowly. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. I'll just -- I'll assist you. You said: "I never really asked Stevanovic where he took the bodies from. At the beginning of the war, most of the bodies were collected from the Luka detention camp and then the centre of town close to the SUP and the hotel Posavina." Now, having seen that in your statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2002, does that assist you or refresh your memory as to information that you received anyway about where the bodies were being collected from, where they were coming from?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you what, as part of the crime department, where I spent my days at that time, there was much discussion about the murders. Therefore, I managed to hear a lot from my work-mates.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I can well understand that, and I'm sure everyone here does, but all I'm asking you is this: Having seen what you said to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2002, that most of the bodies were collected from Luka detention camp, the centre of town close to the SUP and the hotel Posavina, does that assist you now in recalling information that you received about where these bodies came from?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I believe I heard it from my work mates. I heard a lot from them, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm sure you did. I'm sure you did. Some of the things that you heard were that bodies were being collected from Luka, centre of town near the SJB station and this place called the hotel Posavina; correct?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks for that clarification. MR. DI FAZIO: Could we go back to the last photograph I exhibited, please. It's the photo that shows the man, Mr. Stevanovic. Thanks. And could we please just scroll -- I just want to get a bigger look at the bodies, please. A more closer zoom-in view of the bodies. Bottom half of the photograph, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Those people seem to have -- seem to be wearing civilian clothing. Can you tell the Trial Chamber if the people who you saw being buried in May and June and to a lesser extent in early July wore civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: For the most part. A very high per cent of them did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And it's difficult to tell the sex of any of those people, but in that period of time that I just referred to, were some of the people being placed in the mass grave women as well as men?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I seek to tender that photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P143, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you are the only police officer working there apart from other council workers or assistants from the local town, like Mr. Stevanovic -- I'll withdraw that question. Let me ask you this: Did you carry out any identification of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: We would do as follows: When the bodies were brought in, two workers would get them off the truck, and as I had no protective equipment such as gloves, I would ask them to search the bodies and the pockets for any documents. If any documents were retrieved, we used those to ascertain the identity of the corpse. Some of the dead bodies used to be people whom I had known previously and I was able to identify them even without any documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. So other than documentation that was found on the body itself or from knowledge, your own personal knowledge of faces and of people, there was no other way of identifying who went into the grave?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you keep records of the identifications you made?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did you keep the actual documents or objects that allowed you to identify the person? I suppose like driver's licences and identity cards and so on?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: The documents were preserved for awhile in the SUP building, but at some point they began to stink because some of them were covered in blood, and I asked the chief what I was to do with them. He simply said that the documents should be destroyed, burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Chief who precisely? Who was that, is that Veselic or someone else?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Veselic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. So before he died in his car accident, obviously -- I suppose that's self-evident, I won't ask that question. Did you ever -- now, you've told us you kept the records of the identifications you made. Did you ever use those records to produce some sort of permanent record of whatever identifications and numbers of bodies that had gone into that particular grave that you were working at?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you made only one record?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a list which I handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. To whom?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: To one of the supervisors. I think it was the chief, but after this much time it's difficult for me to say who. Someone ordered me to hand it over and I did. Later on, at some point in time, I did see the list again. When I gave my first statement to the OHR, I was shown that list. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Can the witness be shown 65 ter 10131. Both B/C/S and English, please. Thank you. And I'd ask for the Court's indulgence and the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'd just like you, witness, please to have a look at the document as it comes up on the screen. MR. DI FAZIO: Could we have the next page, please. And if we could just go to the top of the document. See what's at the top. If we scroll up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: While we are waiting for that, you can -- there we are. We can see on the English that another date appears, and in the interests of time, and there's no dispute about this, I don't think, this document contains lists of names and dates. Having seen the first and second page at least, is that -- does that contain information that you acquired, you produced, concerning the identities when you were working at the grave?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: The one for the 6th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm talking about the entire document now. Let me ask you this: Is this a document that I showed you some days ago here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Approximately, yes. I don't recall everything precisely, but it was similar to this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is the information that you got when you were carrying out your identifications contained in this document?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Were all of the people that you identified, all of the names you produced, either Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I recall the people of the 6th of May. Franjo Vugrincic was a Croat. I knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: He was one of the people who was buried at the grave that you worked at?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 6th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I also knew Safet Sahrimanovic. He was frequently in prison. Some of them I knew, others I didn't. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I'd like to look at items 114 and then 123, number 123. In the English, 123 appears at -- seven pages in, I believe, and it's under the 24th of May, 1992. And for the B/C/S, well, it's under the 24th of May, 1992, but I'm not sure how many pages in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Number 123 is a chap named Zeljko Malencic, son of Marjan and someone has written, you can see it in the B/C/S version, just to the left of the document - if we scroll to the extreme left - ZNG or Croatian National Guard Corps. Do you know how it was that that one individual happened to be identified as being a member of the ZNG or Croatian National Guard Corps?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I recall that case, he was brought in in a uniform of the Croatian Defence Council or with some other Croatian insignia. He was in uniform and had ID on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And that was something that assisted you in order to conclude this man is a --

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: -- Croatian?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I recall that particular case. I think he was from Rijeka. Yes, it says Rijeka in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If we just scroll back to number 114, that's an item that appears on the 19th of May --

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Number 114 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is reading to himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I could see. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And there we can see that you must have been able to make a note observing that this chap who had died and was going into the grave was dressed in a camouflage uniform and had a band around the head. That must have obviously come from observations you made; correct?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So therefore if the vast majority of these -- if you've been able to carry out observations like this, you would have been able to note if the remainder of the people who went into that grave were in any way combatants because the remainder don't have any -- any combatants, c-o-m-b-a-t-a-n-t-s, because you'd -- the list is -- other than those two --

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I never wrote that down, save for these two ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you ever -- did you ever receive instructions to differentiate between civilians and combatants?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No one gave me any particular instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to observe the wounds on the people who were going into that particular grave?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Many people were covered in blood because they had bullet wounds in the chest or the head. I didn't register each and every such wound, but a high percentage of them had them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, now I come to look at the documents and there's a note dated 18th of May, 1992. It's about five persons, four of them being apparently elderly women. And it says -- there's a note underneath it that says all dead women brought from the morgue died of natural causes. And my question is: Whose note is that exactly? Is that the witness's note or a doctor's or? MR. DI FAZIO: I don't know. And I think the best thing is to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You've heard His Honour's question, can you give us any idea of that particular note, 18th of May? MR. DI FAZIO: Perhaps the B/C/S could go back one day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't recall it. Could I be shown the note, please. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: There it is, you can see it at the bottom of the B/C/S version. 18th of May. 109 to 113, four females and a male, all of a certain age, brought from the morgue. Died of natural causes. Do you know who made that note?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I suppose I typed it out because it seems to be the same typewriter throughout the document. I can't recall it but I think it was in the hospital, that those bodies were taken from the hospital to the morgue and then from the morgue to the location. I suppose the women were Muslim. All brought from the morgue died of natural causes, as it says here. I can't recall the specific cases then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I can assist you in directing your attention to other bits of the document but it may not be necessary. I can tell you that the document has -- and if Your Honours want to see this, it's at 136, 137, item 136 and 137. At some times throughout this document people are listed as being suicides. Do you know how -- how that note came to be made and why people who had committed suicide would be going into this grave?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, objection. It's really calling for speculation. This witness is neither psychiatric or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If I may clarify. I guess the point, if at all relevant, the point would be from whom would the witness receive information that he would then subsequently put into the list. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. That's right. And that's precisely right and I'm certainly not inviting any speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So please don't speculate. But these entries appear, do you know where the information came from? And secondly, do you know, if they were in fact suicides, why they were put into that grave?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Because the Muslim cemetery or the mezar could not be approached since it was in the proximity of some combat activities and the area was mined.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Now, I seek to tender that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P144, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown another document, please. It's 65 ter 258.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness, just so that you can -- you don't need to read it out, by the way. Just have a read of the first page. You see that this is a document dated 22nd October 1992 from Momcilo Mandic and sent to various government entities and personalities. And it says that there is a report attached on the situation in prisons and collection camps in the territory of the Republika Srpska. MR. DI FAZIO: If we go to the next page, please, of both documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And again you can see that it's dated the 22nd of October, to the minister of justice and administration. And it's a report on the situation in prisons and collection camps, prisoners of war, and it deals with various municipalities. Number 1, Vlasenica; 2 is Zvornik. MR. DI FAZIO: If we continue with the English, please. And I think the next page in the B/C/S should take us to Brcko. Number 3. And if that could be made visible for the witness so that he can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just have a look at what it says about Brcko. MR. DI FAZIO: And if -- Your Honours will have to ask for the English to go over to the next page because it doesn't finish on the same page. Okay. May I proceed, Your Honours? Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, the first sentence, the report says: "In the town of Brcko there's no prison or camp for the temporary accommodation of detained enemy soldiers." Then he says that the author of this report says he visited the town to verify a report by the International Red Cross who alleged or were concerned about a large number of citizens of Muslim nationality being liquidated. And the author says that he had a meeting with the most responsible people in Brcko and eventually ascertained that there were five mass graves where a total of 226 people are buried. Thinking back now, are you aware of there being four other graves apart from your own?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Thinking back, can you tell the Trial Chamber how the job that you oversaw, that you personally oversaw continued throughout June and July, was there one hole only into which the bodies were placed or were there more holes created at the same site as time wore on?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was just one. And later on, burials took place in the cemetery. As of the month of July onwards, people were buried in cemeteries.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand that. I'm with you there. But what I'm asking you is this: During May and June when you are carrying out this task of identifying the bodies before they were put into the grave, you must have covered them at some point, surely, with earth, otherwise they would putrify?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately they did putrify and they did smell, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I can understand that. But as that process went on, did you dig any more holes at the same site, the same place you were working at?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: And the number corresponds, 266 persons. If I were to draw a list combining five mass graves, that would correspond. I actually don't think that this is correct. Five mass graves. No, that's not correct, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The author of this report goes on to say these people died during combat activities in Brcko. Since there was a danger of an epidemic, they were buried with religious rites. And the relevant services of interior ministry and other services carried out the identification of dead people on several occasions. Are you aware of anyone else in Brcko, any other police officer from the interior ministry carrying out identification of dead people other than yourself?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And we don't need to look at the screen but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: We don't need to look at the screen but the author of this report is some person named Slobodan Avlijas. Have you ever heard of the person?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Slobodan?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Avlijas?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No, it doesn't ring a bell. I've never heard of a family name like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours, please, I would either -- my first application is to admit the document fully in evidence, but again if you are not with me, I'd ask for it be marked for identification. And there will be further evidence later in the case concerning this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P145, marked for identification, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown 65 ter 10132. It's a handwritten note.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness, the document that I showed you earlier, the list of names of identified people, that runs from May -- 1st of May to the 10th of July. I'm sorry. I'm sorry, let me rephrase that. I mislead you. It runs from the 5th of May to the 10th of July. And on my calculations it's got about -- has got 216 people. So this note may or may not refer to your list. First question is this: Do you recognise the handwriting or do you know --

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I believe that this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It's yours?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I think so but I think roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: There's no one better qualified to tell us than you. That's your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: I think so. I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, in that case, can you tell us how it was that you came to write this note; why; for what reason?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: That I can't recall. Buried in mass grave, 216 total; identified, 103; died of natural causes, 8; female bodies, 9. The people killed were buried at the cemetery properly marked and with religious rites. Maybe as I was handing over the list to somebody, to the chief or somebody, it doesn't really matter, maybe I also compiled this note. But I can't recall. I can't ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. MR. DI FAZIO: And I ask for this to be fully admitted into evidence, and I can tell the Trial Chamber that there will be other evidence about this particular document

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, before we hear Mr. Pantelic, can you clarify with the witness the meaning of the second addition at the bottom of the note that says that: "The people killed were buried at a cemetery, properly marked and with religious rites." Because I'm not sure I completely have understood the sequence of events here. Did the witness first take part in the opening of a mass grave and then identify the bodies and then have them reburied somewhere else, or can you clarify -- MR. DI FAZIO: I will. I don't think that's the scenario but I'll ask the witness to describe -- to provide us with the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Firstly, the mass grave that you worked at in May and June and early July of 1992, they were people who had been killed and were being brought directly to that grave, they hadn't been exhumed or taken out of graves elsewhere, as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, an objection. There is a discrepancy between the original in B/C/S and the translation. My learned friend from the Prosecution uses the term "killed." However, in the handwritten text it says "buried," not "killed." However, in the English version I can see the word "killed" instead of "buried," and that's what the Prosecutor is using. I don't think that the witness, if this is indeed his document, did not use the term "killed."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about this word [B/C/S spoken], this is not the term I would use. I have my doubts now as to whether I really authored this document. I don't think so. I would never have used this term [B/C/S spoken] "buried." I'm in doubts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Be it at it may, the word [B/C/S spoken] does not correspond with the word "killed."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, this is not the word that I would have used.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please let me finish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's cut through this. Could the witness please read out from the last parts -- the last paragraph and then hear what the interpreters have to say about it. Then we'll have an interpretation directly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Starting with the 10th of July, 1992, [B/C/S spoken] buried at a certain cemetery properly marked in keeping with religious rites.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's remark the word [B/C/S spoken] almost cannot be translated into English. It means "pushed" and it's out of the context completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, Your Honour. The word [B/C/S spoken] in B/C/S means like when some of members of Trial Chamber are familiar with that, like when we are launching a new ship into the sea, Your Honour. So that means word [B/C/S spoken]. You know, like we have in shipyard new and it's going to the sea. So I really cannot find exact word in English, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ignjic, is that the word that you said that you would never use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. I don't -- no, I don't think I would ever use this word, [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We won't get any further with this. MR. DI FAZIO: No, no, Your Honours. I'm grateful to Mr. Pantelic for his assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But let me go back to my question, which actually had nothing to do with this document. It was answering a query that His Honour Judge Harhoff had asked, and that's this: The people who you were -- who were going into the mass grave in May and June and July whom you were sometimes identifying, had they been killed or died somewhere and been brought directly to the site, or had they been exhumed from somewhere and taken once again to be buried a second time?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Directly brought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ignjic, what I don't fully understand yet is you then met the bodies in that mass grave to which the bodies were brought directly, that's what you are saying. You then proceeded to try and identify the bodies that were brought to that mass grave; is that correct? And once you had identified them to the extent that you could, what would then happen to the bodies? Would then they be left in the mass graves for some time and then taken to the cemetery or what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let me explain. When that truck brought the dead bodies from any part of the town, before they were put in that hole that had been dug out, before that we tried to identify them, and when that was done, they would be lowered into that hole or pit. And then as far as I know, that hole was sealed after the 10th of July or some date around that time in July. And I don't know what happened after that to those bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm sorry to spend time on this, but if I understand you correctly, then the bodies remained in the mass grave and then at some later point somebody else took them to a cemetery and had them properly buried; is that correct? Or is it a fact that you simply don't know what happened? In any case, what brought you to add the second paragraph on your note that the people who were pushed were buried at a cemetery properly marked and with religious rites. Can you tell us briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the 1st of May until the 7th of -- or 10th of July, all the dead bodies of non-Serbians lying around the town were buried in that mass grave. And I'm giving you approximate dates. After the 10th of July, the authorities were re-established. In town when a dead body was found, the investigating judge and prosecutor would come to the site. There would be investigation. Doctors came from Doboj to carry out postmortems, and then people were buried in cemeteries after having undergone that procedure. And the burials were carried out in accordance with procedure. Anything that happened between the 1st of May and the 10th of July people were buried in the mass grave. People were not buried in a proper way in proper cemeteries. It only started happening after the 10th of July, not before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, all of this leads to the question: Who organised the burial in the mass grave up until 10th July, and who organised the burial in the cemeteries after the 10th of July? Which authority organised all of this, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it was the authorities, but I don't know who exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? Was it the municipal authorities or was it the police or was it the army or -- who took care of all of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just to follow on from His Honour's question, were you ever present at any exhumation and reburial?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: Many times before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. But I'm talking about the people at the grave-site that we've been talking about this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And how do you know it occurred?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. What I'm asking is this: Your note indicates that the people were buried at a cemetery properly marked with religious rites. You didn't attend any exhumation and reburial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I think there is a misunderstanding here. If I understood the witness correct, the second paragraph refers to other bodies, not to the bodies that were in the mass grave. That's bodies that were found or collected after the 10th of July. And they were buried properly. That's what this tends to say. MR. DI FAZIO: I must have misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You just heard His Honour. His Honour has got the correct understanding and I don't; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CVJETKO IGNJIC
utterances.text: His, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm grateful to Your Honour for that. I might just alter my order of documents at the moment and just utilise the last five minutes because I will have about another 20 minutes in the morning, if Your Honours, please, or 15 minutes. Can the witness be shown 65 ter 33, please. Has the note been given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, it now will be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P146, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, I'm not objecting to -- for the admission of this exhibit if you are speaking about this note where witness was not a hundred per cent sure whether that was his handwriting or not. I would suggest that this witness now in this courtroom make his writings of the same text which is on the document and then Defence could forward it to graphologist or a handwriting expert in order to be a hundred per cent sure whether that was his handwriting or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, may I just ask you, do you contest the information provided in the note, because the only thing of importance are the numbers there, that there were 216 persons in total, 103 were identified, 8 died of natural causes, and 9 of them were females. That's the substance of the note which the Chamber needs to take into account at a later stage. Now, if you want to challenge those figures, then of course we can proceed through the procedure that you'd -- but if you are fine with the figures, then I don't see the point in having a graphologist to check whether this was or was not his handwriting. That's, in my view, unimportant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If your opinion, Your Honour, is that it's not relevant, then I cannot say nothing but to admit. But it's a matter of principal, you know. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It's the information -- sorry to interrupt you. It's the information contained in the note that is relevant. And if you agree that this is relevant and you don't contest the substance of that information, if you agree with the numbers that are there, then I don't see the need to proceed to a graphological examination of whether this is or is not his handwriting. Because in the end what matters is the figures that are contained therein. And if you are fine with them, then I suggest we just drop it and take the information for what it is, whoever drafted it. MR. DI FAZIO: Could I be of some assistance to Mr. Pantelic. I have I'm sure I can be. We've already heard that the witness said it was his handwriting and then later had reservations about an expression used in the document. But there will be other evidence in the case about that note, and Mr. Pantelic may want to revisit the whole issue after that other evidence in the case has come -- has been presented to you, and Mr. Pantelic has had an opportunity of observing it, so why don't we put the issue on ice. He can always revisit it later, having heard all of the evidence concerning the note.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I agree with this approach. Yes, sure. We shall have time to challenge that then. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I'm always glad to be of assistance. Now if we could have 65 -- I note the time, Your Honours. It might be -- it's quarter past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, rather than embarking on a new line, we'll take the adjournment to tomorrow morning. To the witness, you are now sworn as a witness in this case and I am obliged to caution you that you cannot discuss -- you cannot speak to the lawyers from either side in this matter and in your conversations with anybody else you cannot discuss your testimony that you are giving here. Do you understand what I've just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So you would be required to return to this Chamber tomorrow morning at 9.00 when your examination-in-chief by Mr. Di Fazio will continue. Pleasant evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, if you could just clarify one other thing. The Prosecution has filed a motion on 14th of October seeking to change the mode of testimony of three witnesses, ST-52, ST-79, and ST-4, and it is unclear it me in the motion whether the testimony of the last of these three witnesses, ST-4, who originally was listed as a 92 bis witness, whether you wish to have him or her transferred to a 92 ter or to a viva voce, and I'd kindly ask you to clarify tomorrow. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll get -- either I'll address you or Ms. Korner will in the morning and we'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understand that tomorrow morning we resume in Courtroom I. Thank you.
